Tech Report: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1625 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, after eight years in space and a journey covering 10 billion kilometers, a pioneering X-ray telescope traveling to Mercury has captured its first observations of a distant cosmic object.
  • Scientists at the University of Leicester are now evaluating the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), which is traveling aboard the two-spacecraft mission.
  • Industry observers note that the telescope has spent eight years traveling through space, making it essential to confirm that its delicate components are still working properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, after eight years in space and a journey covering 10 billion kilometers, a pioneering X-ray telescope traveling to Mercury has captured its first observations of a distant cosmic object. The instrument, built in the UK, successfully detected X-rays from the Crab Nebula, one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky, marking an vital milestone for the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's BepiColombo mission.

Scientists at the University of Leicester are now evaluating the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), which is traveling aboard the two-spacecraft mission. Their initial results are highly encouraging, arriving just as BepiColombo prepares to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21.

Industry observers note that the telescope has spent eight years traveling through space, making it essential to confirm that its delicate components are still working properly. Although engineers monitored MIXS throughout the journey, the instrument could not look directly into space until September. That opportunity came after the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) separated from the two science orbiters, the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mercury Magnetosphere Orbiter (MMO) or Mio.

With its view finally unobstructed, MIXS could begin the critical tests needed before the spacecraft enters its planned orbit around the solar system's smallest planet.

A Telescope's First Look Across 6,500 Light-Years.

Recent findings suggest that for its first astronomical target, the team selected the Crab Nebula, located approximately 6,500 light-years from Earth. This well-studied remnant of an exploded star produces a strong, predictable X-ray signal, making it an ideal reference for testing the telescope's performance.

Recent findings suggest that by examining how MIXS observes this distant object, researchers can determine whether the instrument still performs as expected after its lengthy journey. They can also compare the results with laboratory measurements collected in 2015, when the telescope was last tested on Earth.

According to recent reports, the main observation campaign took place on September 11 and 12. Over 39 hours, the spacecraft carried out 55 carefully controlled changes in orientation to collect the data.

According to recent reports, one vital measurement was the telescope's angular resolution, which describes its ability to distinguish small details in an image. Scientists determined this by examining how widely the Crab Nebula's X-ray signal spread across the detector. Remarkably, MIXS delivered slightly sharper resolution than it had during its laboratory tests in 2015.

That improvement is particularly encouraging because the instrument will eventually use its X-ray vision to investigate the composition of Mercury's surface.

Better Than Expected After Eight Years in Space.

Professor Emma Bunce, Principal Investigator (PI) for MIXS and Director of the Institute for Space at the University of Leicester, welcomed the results as a major achievement for the international team responsible for developing the instrument.

Professor Bunce noted: "We have waited a long time to make measurements with MIXS and it is fantastic to see it operating brilliantly in space. This is testament to our engineering and technical team, and our international partners who we have worked with over many years to build this incredible instrument. 80% of the technology on MIXS is new!

Industry observers note that "During our calibration observations we have determined that MIXS is generally performing fantastically well in space! We have no effects in our images that are associated with 'stray light' (optical photons getting in when they should not). We continue to see effects of galactic cosmic rays as we did during cruise, but we understand these and can filter them out. We see some self-fluorescence which appears when the Sun is illuminating the optic, but this won't affect our dayside observations of Mercury's surface. And the detector has suffered no radiation damage after 8 years in space.

"We see some effects in the instrument that we are still studying and expect to undertake some optimization procedures during the Mercury commissioning phase to fine tune MIXS in preparation for the science phase.".

Industry observers note that the results suggest that the telescope has weathered its long exposure to the harsh space environment exceptionally well. Engineers have found no unwanted visible light interfering with its images, and the effects of high-energy cosmic rays are understood well enough to be removed during data processing.

The team has also identified a small amount of X-ray emission originating within the instrument itself when sunlight strikes its optics. However, this effect is not expected to interfere with observations of Mercury's sunlit surface. Most importantly, the detector shows no signs of radiation damage after eight years in space.

Some remaining effects still require investigation, and scientists expect to make further adjustments after the spacecraft reaches Mercury to ensure that MIXS is ready for its full scientific mission.

How X-Rays Will Reveal Mercury's Hidden Chemistry.

In a recent development, bepiColombo is designed to investigate Mercury in unprecedented detail. As the smallest and one of the least explored rocky planets in our solar system, Mercury offers scientists a rare opportunity to understand how planets form and change under the extreme conditions found close to a star.

Industry observers note that one of the mission's major goals is to uncover the planet's chemical composition and geological history. These findings could help explain Mercury's unusual characteristics while providing broader insights into the formation and evolution of the solar system.

MIXS, carried aboard the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), will play a central role in this investigation. Developed by a European consortium led by the University of Leicester, it draws on the university's long history of X-ray astronomy research.

Sources indicate that it is the first imaging X-ray telescope to operate on a planetary science mission. Working alongside other scientific instruments, MIXS will help produce a global map showing the elements that make up Mercury's surface, revealing its atomic composition in greater detail than ever before. It is also the only UK-led scientific instrument aboard BepiColombo and receives support from the UK Space Agency.

According to recent reports, the instrument works by detecting fluorescent X-rays released by rocks on Mercury's surface. When powerful X-rays from the Sun strike these rocks, they can cause atoms within the material to emit X-rays of their own. Different elements produce characteristic X-ray signals, allowing scientists to identify what the surface is made of without collecting physical samples.

MIXS will make these measurements with assistance from the Solar Intensity X-ray and particle Spectrometer (SIXS), which monitors the solar radiation and particles reaching Mercury.

The telescope will also examine X-rays emitted from Mercury's nighttime surface when charged particles associated with the planet's magnetic environment strike it. These measurements could reveal important connections between Mercury's surface and the surrounding space environment.

A 10 Billion Kilometer Journey With a Personal Legacy.

According to recent reports, for Dr. Adrian Martindale, MIXS Instrument Scientist at the University of Leicester's School of Physics and Astronomy, the successful observations represent the culmination of more than two decades of work.

Martindale joined the project in 2003 while still an undergraduate student and has been involved in nearly every aspect of the instrument's development.

Sources indicate that dr. Martindale noted: "BepiColombo, and MIXS in particular, are like part of my family. I've been involved since I was an undergraduate and touched almost every part of the instrument before it was released.

According to recent reports, "This first data is mind-blowing to me. The last time we could see through this telescope it was in the basement under the School of Physics and Astronomy in Leicester, but after a rocket launch, eight years in space and 10 billion kilometers traveled it looks just the same. I can't wait to see the science data it produces when we get into orbit.".

Sources indicate that the milestone also carries special meaning for the team because MIXS represents the scientific legacy of Professor George Fraser. Fraser was the instrument's original Principal Investigator and the driving force behind its innovative optical design before his death in March 2014.

Professor Bunce added: "We are thinking of George as we operate MIXS fully in space for the first time and know that he would be very, very proud of the team and delighted at our first light observations.".

BepiColombo Prepares for Its Final Arrival at Mercury.

BepiColombo began its arrival phase on September 3, when the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) separated from the spacecraft assembly.

The remaining connected spacecraft are scheduled to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21. The two science orbiters, MPO and Mio, are then expected to separate on December 9 to 10, allowing them to prepare for their respective scientific operations.

In a recent development, the mission's primary science phase is scheduled to begin in April 2027. Once underway, BepiColombo will investigate Mercury's surface, internal structure, magnetic field, and surrounding environment, helping scientists piece together the history of a planet that remains surprisingly mysterious despite its proximity to the Sun.

For the MIXS team, the successful first observations of the Crab Nebula offer an early indication of what the instrument may accomplish when it finally turns its attention to Mercury.

International Collaboration and Funding.

Recent findings suggest that MIXS was developed through a partnership involving research institutions and technology companies across Europe. Participating organizations include:.

UK funding for the BepiColombo MIXS instrument comes from the UK Space Agency, which serves as the lead funding organization, along with STFC, the European Space Agency, and the University of Leicester.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • FIFA have confirmed the hosts for the 2031 and 2035 Women's World Cup.
  • The United States, along with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, made an uncontested bid to host in 2031.
  • FIFA's revenue for the 2026 men's World Cup was around $15 billion (€13.7 billion), and it's clear that US Soccer feels that hosting the women's tournament is the next move forward.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FIFA have confirmed the hosts for the 2031 and 2035 Women's World Cup.

The United States, along with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, made an uncontested bid to host in 2031. It will be the first tournament to feature 48 teams — as is the case with the men. The US has hosted the event twice before, in 2003 and 1999, and is also the most successful country in its history, having won it four times.

FIFA's revenue for the 2026 men's World Cup was around $15 billion (€13.7 billion), and it's clear that US Soccer feels that hosting the women's tournament is the next move forward. With the women's domestic league (NWSL) considered the strongest in the world and the US national team so dominant, securing the tournament in 2031 is a further sign of the US' committment to women's football.

"We expect and strategy for the 2031 Women’s World Cup to be the largest women’s sporting event in history," Emily Cosler, US Soccer’s vice-president of strategy told The Guardian.

Sources indicate that the 2035 tournament was also awarded to the sole bidders, England, Scotland, Northern Ireland and Wales. This sees the World Cup return to the United Kingdom for the first time since 1966, the only time England's men's team won the competition. The women lost the 2023 final to Spain. It also means that the UK will host two major tournaments in relatively quick succession, with the men's 2028 European Championships also set to be held in England, Scotland and Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the tournament would bring "visitors, investment and jobs to every part of the country.".

Sources indicate that given that FIFA President Gianni Infantino had revealed last year that both bids were unchallenged, this news comes as little surprise. Nevertheless, with the hosts now official, a 48-team tournament marks a remarkable advance for the women's game. The 2011 World Cup in Germany had just 16 teams.

Recent findings suggest that the next World Cup will be in Brazil in 2027, running from June 24 to July 25. . Eighteen of the 32 teams have already secured qualification, including Germany.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Well, NASA astronaut Anil Menon will, anyway.
  • Sources indicate that "We need plants to survive as we set up our moon base, and as we go to Mars, we're going to have to grow our own nutrition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The astronauts on the International Space Station will celebrate Thanksgiving with some nontraditional fare.

Well, NASA astronaut Anil Menon will, anyway. In a video the agency released on Monday (Nov. 23), Menon highlighted off some of the plants he and his crewmates are growing in orbit and told us what's in store for the greens.

Sources indicate that "We need plants to survive as we set up our moon base, and as we go to Mars, we're going to have to grow our own nutrition. So that's what we're doing this Thanksgiving," Menon said in the 2.5-minute video.

According to recent reports, "I proposal on using this [plant] with a tortilla and some pasta and some hot sauce to make my Thanksgiving meal," added Menon, who was wearing a chef's toque for the occasion. "And I'm grateful for you and for my family at home.".

He passed the microphone to fellow NASA astronaut Luke Delaney, who didn't talk about food but expressed gratitude to his family, crewmates and support network on Earth.

Next up was NASA's Jessica Watkins, who gave us a rundown of the broader Thanksgiving menu in space.

According to recent reports, "Some of what we'll be eating here — we've got some roasted turkey, some mac and cheese, some mashed potatoes, and some candied yams," Watkins stated, showing off the small bags containing each of those comestibles. "So, we should be in good shape.".

The Canadian Space Agency's (CSA) Joshua Kutryk spoke next. He said he'll eat rice and the space-grown plants, which he'll consume raw "because it reminds me of Earth, which I miss.".

All four of the astronauts then wished us a happy Thanksgiving and did some zero-g flips and rolls, sending the space plants on a bit of a ride.

Delaney, Kutryk and Watkins are members of SpaceX's Crew-13 mission, which arrived at the International Space Station (ISS) on Oct. 1. There's a fourth Crew-13 astronaut as well — Sergey Teteryatnikov, of the Russian space agency Roscosmos.

That quartet shares the ISS with Menon and cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina, who arrived in July aboard a Russian Soyuz spacecraft.

Astronauts tend to get major holidays off on the ISS, and to celebrate them together. Doing so reinforces the already-strong bonds the crewmates share and helps them deal with the pain of being away from friends and family, which can be especially acute on holidays like Thanksgiving and Christmas.

It has been revealed that kutryk is likely feeling especially emotional these days. On Tuesday, the CSA revealed that Kutryk's wife had given birth to the couple's third child, a daughter.

Sources indicate that "Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our fresh little star into our lives," the couple mentioned in a statement shared by the CSA. "We are very proud of our growing family and are looking forward to getting our little crew of five all reunited.".

#139347. Industry News: NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1647 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA's Voyager 1 has achieved another extraordinary milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth.
  • It has been revealed that the historic moment occurred on November 18 at 2:16 a.m.
  • The achievement marks another remarkable chapter for a probe that has traveled farther than any other human-made object, survived decades beyond its original mission, and continues to explore a region of space that no spacecraft had previously entered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA's Voyager 1 has achieved another extraordinary milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth. After more than 49 years of traveling through space, humanity's most distant spacecraft is now approximately 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from home. At that distance, even a signal moving at the speed of light needs an entire day to make the journey.

It has been revealed that the historic moment occurred on November 18 at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST). Scientists and engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, which is managed by Caltech, received a signal from Voyager 1 early Thursday, exactly 24 hours after the spacecraft reached the milestone.

The achievement marks another remarkable chapter for a probe that has traveled farther than any other human-made object, survived decades beyond its original mission, and continues to explore a region of space that no spacecraft had previously entered.

Voyager 1 Is Now 24 Light-Hours From Earth.

Recent findings suggest that astronomers often describe enormous cosmic distances in terms of how long light takes to travel them. A light-day represents the distance light covers in 24 hours, or roughly 16.1 billion miles.

Light moves through a vacuum at approximately 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) per second. To put Voyager 1's distance in perspective, sunlight passing Earth takes only about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon. Reaching Neptune takes roughly four hours, while traveling from Neptune to Voyager 1 requires another 20 hours.

Even these enormous distances are small compared with those separating stars. A single light-year, the distance light travels in one year, measures approximately 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers).

It has been revealed that voyager 1's extraordinary distance also creates a major challenge for mission controllers. Sending a command to the spacecraft now requires 24 hours, and receiving a response takes another 24 hours. A complete exchange therefore spans two full days, even though the signals travel at the fastest speed possible.

Recent findings suggest that the milestone comes as engineers investigate a communication problem. NASA has not received scientific or engineering data from Voyager 1 since November 14. However, the probe continues transmitting a carrier signal, the radio signal that normally carries information back to Earth. By tracking this signal and calculating the spacecraft's trajectory, mission specialists were able to verify that Voyager 1 had crossed the one light-day mark. Engineers are continuing to investigate why the expected data is not coming through.

A Historic Journey Beyond the Solar System's Planets.

Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, were launched in 1977 to take advantage of an unusual arrangement of the outer planets. The alignment allowed the spacecraft to use planetary gravity to travel from one destination to another, making an ambitious exploration mission possible.

It has been revealed that managed by JPL, the Voyagers became the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn. They also delivered the first high-resolution images of these distant planets, revealing extraordinary latest details about their atmospheres, rings, and moons. Voyager 2 continued farther, becoming the first spacecraft to explore Uranus and Neptune up close.

Recent findings suggest that today, both probes are traveling through interstellar space, making them humanity's only spacecraft to have crossed into the region beyond the Sun's protective bubble. Their instruments continue monitoring changes in the Sun's magnetic field across immense distances, providing scientists with measurements that cannot be collected from Earth.

In a recent development, "Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets," said Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. "But it went on to become central to NASA's fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.".

According to recent reports, "Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery," noted Dave Gallagher, JPL director. "Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward latest frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.".

Voyager's Golden Record Carries a Message From Earth.

In a recent development, the Voyager spacecraft carry more than scientific instruments. Each also holds a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph record containing images and sounds representing life on Earth. These recordings were designed as messages that an advanced extraterrestrial civilization might discover someday.

The records give the mission a purpose extending far beyond its scientific discoveries. Even after the spacecraft eventually lose the ability to communicate with Earth, they will continue traveling through space with a small collection of sights and sounds from the planet that launched them.

"Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward," remarked Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. "Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.".

Exploring the Mysterious Region Beyond the Sun.

Voyager 1 is presently moving through space at approximately 38,000 mph (61,155 kph). In 2012, it became the first spacecraft to cross the boundary of the heliosphere, a vast region surrounding the Sun that is filled with particles and magnetic fields generated by our star.

This protective bubble helps shield the solar system from cosmic radiation arriving from elsewhere in the galaxy. Beyond its outer boundary lies interstellar space, where particles and magnetic fields from the broader galaxy become more dominant.

Voyager 2 followed a different route and crossed into interstellar space in 2018. Together, the probes are providing the first direct observations of conditions beyond the heliosphere.

Recent findings suggest that one of their most intriguing discoveries is that the Sun's effects do not simply disappear at the boundary. Its influence appears to extend much farther into interstellar space than scientists once understood, raising newly introduced questions about where the environment shaped by our star truly gives way to the surrounding galaxy.

In a recent development, "The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere," remarked Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. "One big surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.".

How NASA Is Keeping Voyager 1 Alive After Nearly 50 Years.

Operating spacecraft built nearly half a century ago requires increasingly inventive engineering. Both Voyagers have experienced problems as their equipment ages, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer. NASA engineers have repeatedly developed solutions that allow the probes to continue working despite these setbacks.

Electricity has become one of the mission's greatest limitations. Earlier in 2026, engineers took a calculated risk by switching off three devices aboard Voyager 1 and replacing them with three alternatives that consume less power. This change was intended to help the spacecraft stretch its remaining energy supply.

In a recent development, voyager 1 depends on a radioisotope thermal generator that is now approximately 50 years old. Often described as a nuclear battery, the device produces electricity by converting heat released during the radioactive decay of plutonium.

As the radioactive material continues to decay, the available power gradually decreases. Both Voyager spacecraft lose approximately four watts of electrical output every year, forcing engineers to make difficult decisions about which systems can remain operational.

The latest conservation measures are expected to provide enough power to operate the spacecraft's current scientific instruments until at least the summer of 2027, when both probes will celebrate their 50th launch anniversaries.

One Day, Voyager 1 Will Become a Silent Messenger to the Stars.

Sources indicate that maintaining contact across such staggering distances requires some of NASA's most powerful communications equipment. The agency relies on its Deep Space Network, a worldwide system of large radio antennas located at three facilities, to communicate with Voyager and other spacecraft traveling to and beyond the Moon.

Sources indicate that despite the enormous communication delay and the spacecraft's aging systems, engineers continue monitoring Voyager 1 daily and transmitting instructions every week. The mission remains an extraordinary demonstration of what long-term spacecraft engineering can achieve.

According to recent reports, "We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to," said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. "Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity's silent ambassador to the stars.".

A good bed frame can improve the look of your room, but it also contributes to sleep hygiene and extends the life of your mattress. I've rounded up the team's favorites below, with prices reflecting queen-size frames where applicable.

In a recent development, be sure to check out our other sleep guides, including the Best Mattresses, Best Hybrid Mattresses, Best Japanese Joinery Bed Frames, Best Bedsheets, and Best Sleep Gifts for more. And if you don't want to upgrade your frame just yet, check out this advice on how to fix bed frame problems.

Updated November 2026: We've added newly introduced bed frames from Castlery and Quince. We've also checked for accuracy throughout.

I've owned the Thuma Classic Bed for five years, and it feels as good as newly introduced. You don't need a single tool to assemble this solid wood bed frame. The firm uses traditional Japanese joinery techniques, and it took me about 15 minutes to put the whole thing together. That means disassembly and reassembly when I had to move was so easy—there are just two thumb screws at the top and bottom edges of the frame, which you can tighten by hand once everything else is in place.

More surprising is how sturdy it is. I've gone through so many bed frames before the Thuma, and after a year or two, there's usually a broken slat or bent metal rod here and there. Or the slats keep falling down, so you have to do that thing where you pull the mattress over your head as you try to shove them back in place (just me?). The Thuma doesn't creak and never slides around. The foam Pillowboard is an additional expense, but it's comfy. Thuma has since added a wood headboard, which is pricier, but that's what I'll probably upgrade to next, since it completes the look. The only downside is how expensive this whole bed frame is (the price has jumped since I first purchased it), but if it helps, the Thuma is made from repurposed wood, and it's UL GreenGuard Gold Certified, meaning low chemical emissions. —Julian Chokkattu.

Thuma made its name with a minimalist wooden bed (our top pick, above) with clean lines and a tool-free assembly process that's no more complex than snapping together Lego bricks. The Signature was rolled out in February 2025 as the brand's first fully upholstered bed. The Thuma Signature has the same Japanese wood joinery at its heart for easy assembly, but covers the frame in soft Italian felted wool or performance linen for a decidedly more posh experience. I've been testing the wool version for a few months. It took less than five minutes for me to assemble, and it's very solid and dead silent, with no squeaking whatsoever. The plush headboard upholstery is pillow-soft, and my only problem with it is remembering not to just lay my head directly on it. Best of all, when it's time to move, this bed pops apart in just a few minutes without any bolts or screws. —Martin Cizmar.

DreamCloud (queen, with bamboo headboard).

It has been revealed that I really admire Japanese joinery bed frames, not just because of their minimalistic beauty but also their easy, tool-free setup. Trust me, we don’t want my clumsiness around sharp objects. Not all bed frames that follow this blueprint are of the same caliber, with some being far more stable than others, and the price point usually reflects that. DreamCloud's bamboo Japanese joinery bed frame wasn’t just gorgeous, but outfitted with small details that make a big impact. These include tiny additional rods on each of the boards, located where they are stacked atop each other at the ends. The idea is to keep each of the rails that make up the frame even more secure than just the tension of the overall design. There are included foam blocks if you decide to throw in a headboard, so there's no banging against the wall, either. Plus, I’ll never argue with the price tag, which is very within my budget. —Julia Forbes.

I was broker than broke when I got my first apartment more than a decade ago, and this cheap bed frame I bought from Amazon is still being circulated among my younger family members. It's as simple as simple gets, but the steel construction means the frame is durable, and you don't need to add a box spring. The 18-inch model leaves a cavernous space beneath the bed that can accommodate several tote-style storage containers—which could be a blessing or a curse depending on the usual state of your bedroom floor. Just keep in mind that there is no edge whatsoever. This thing is basically a table for your mattress, but it'll get the job done.

I've tested nearly a dozen different bed frames during my time leading this coverage area for the WIRED Reviews team, and the Saatva Siena is probably the prettiest and most elegant I've ever tried. The leather upholstery just makes it feel so grown-up. It's sexy but not straight out of a dark romance dungeon. It's a statement piece that blends in with my decor. I like the free in-room delivery and the rich smell of leather. However, while the frame itself is exceedingly stable, it does slide around on my hardwood floors (I'm planning on attaching some rubbery grips to the feet to remedy this). My main complaint is that you can see the slats of the frame when you're close to the mattress. From a distance, it looks OK, but the white slats are so obvious up close, if you're looking, that it takes away from the whole put-together effect for me. It's also the perfect awkward height to attract dust bunnies that can be difficult to clean unless you move the bed to sweep or vacuum. Overall, these drawbacks are minor, and I still think this frame is worth your consideration. I'll just cross my fingers that none of my Hinge dates look too closely.

When the crib phase ends, this is the bed to get. I upgraded my son from a crib that converted into a toddler bed into this actual kids’ bed, and everyone is sleeping better for it. Nestig originally caught my eye for its adjustable crib, and the Nestig Wave Kids Bed shares similar design elements, with its wooden headboard and side panels. This bed frame can be used as either a Montessori-style floor bed or a standard twin, depending on whether you add the legs. It can accommodate a variety of twin-sized mattresses, and my son loves climbing into his bed each night and demanding I lie down with him while we read. The floor bed aspect is handy since I quietly roll out of the bed and onto the floor to escape his grip, and I like knowing that if my son rolled out of bed, he doesn’t have far to go. When it's time to add the legs, I'll have to take the frame apart partially, which is a small con but not a deal-breaker. —Nena Farrell.

Small bedroom? Mobility issues? Don’t want to block a window? You might want to consider a low-profile frame. They’re typically under 11 inches high as opposed to around 20 inches for a traditional frame, which means you may not get as much under-bed storage, but for many, the benefits outweigh this drawback. (The Cooper has about 7 inches of clearance off the floor.) I personally have been grappling with not wanting to block a large window with a headboard, and I was curious if a low-profile frame might be the answer. Sure enough, it was—this 38-inch-tall frame hits just 2 inches below the windowsill and looks fantastic. In fact, the minimalist, mid-century-inspired Cooper is practically indistinguishable from similar frames being sold by Pottery Barn and Crate and Barrel, but runs around $500 less.

Sources indicate that with its angled legs and rounded corners, the Cooper definitely has Thuma vibes, but does not feature Japanese joinery construction. It requires some assembly; namely, joining the rails together and screwing down the slats. If you’d rather not deal with this, white-glove delivery is available for $199. For my test unit, it took the delivery driver about 20 minutes to assemble, and in the few months I’ve had it, there haven’t been any squeaks, creaks, or loosening hardware. Note that an 8- to 12-inch mattress is recommended. —Kat Merck.

Recent findings suggest that if you prefer the look of fabric covers, the Awara Platform frame will be a good fit. It's simple to assemble, and the pieces are easy to move. The spruce wooden slats are all attached together, so once you have the four frame pieces assembled, simply roll the slats out and they'll attach via hook-and-loop closures to the frame itself. The frame's height is nice, too. It's elevated just enough to make your bed look refined, but not so much that you'll end up losing things underneath your mattress. Though be aware, I did seem to stub my toes on this bed frame more than others I've tested.

This adjustable base is from the makers of one of our favorite mattresses overall and one of our favorite mattresses for side sleepers. It runs on electricity to move the hydraulic-like motors below, which raise both the head and foot area of the bed. It comes with a wireless Bluetooth-enabled remote with buttons to adjust the head and foot portion of the bed up and down, a built-in flashlight, and a button to bring the frame down to a flat level.

Industry observers note that the Legget & Platt app can act as a remote as well—a huge sigh of relief for a generally scatterbrained person like myself who's prone to losing things. In the app, you name your bed, make the adjustments, and save your favorite positions so you can easily go back to them. The bed frame is sleek—not bulky at all—and is around 13 inches off the ground, making extra storage space underneath that I didn’t have before. The legs are virtually invisible, although the zero-clearance design allows the base to be used without the legs if using platform bases.

It has been revealed that the adjustable frame rises in half-inch increments from 13 to 18 inches from the original base, and the motor is fairly quiet. The base works with mattresses designed to flex, without shifting inside materials or weakening the structure, and is compatible with nearly all Saatva mattresses. For non-Saatva mattresses, check with the manufacturer to ensure it's compatible with an adjustable base.

Recent findings suggest that saatva provides a 10-year warranty as well as free in-room delivery and setup, and the deliverymen were done in less than 15 minutes, even putting my old mattress back on for me. I often work in my bed and use pillows to prop me up, and this took away the need to be surrounded by a dozen or so of my favorite body pillows. This customizable frame would work great for those with mobility problems or health issues like acid reflux, restless leg syndrome, sleep apnea, or sciatica (among other things). This bougie bed base isn’t completely necessary for me, but it’s a fun luxury to have. —Molly Higgins.

Recent findings suggest that this bed frame took me an entire day to build, but it was worth it. It has versions with and without storage, and I chose a storage version to fill the drawers with my various bedding. Adding the storage does nearly double the price and adds to your building time, but the drawers are really useful if it’s something you want. It’s a beautiful bed frame that's felt very stable for the two months I’ve been sleeping on it so far. Even with my questionable building skills, there hasn’t been a squeak when I’m sleeping or getting into bed.

Sources indicate that you will want to add on a slatted bed base from Ikea for full support if you don’t have a mattress base already. I really liked pairing this frame with the Lönset slatted bed base for great support on my back. There’s also the cheaper Luröy base if you’re on a budget. —Nena Farrell.

Sources indicate that I don't say this lightly or often, but I feel like Silk & Snow could charge much more for this Oeko-Tex-certified bed frame. Assembly was annoying—give me video instructions or give me death!—and slightly fiddly, with many individual pieces that you need to screw in or slot together. But the frame is sturdy, the upholstered fabric is soft and durable, and the slats are nice and supportive. The best feature is the built-in storage drawer, which slides out smoothly and closes tightly with magnets. It strikes the perfect balance of form and function.

Sources indicate that it doesn't have as much storage space as the lift-up option we recommend from Castlery, but there's room for spare linens, off-season clothing, or certain unmentionables that you don't want lying around out in the open. Be aware that closing the drawer while your bedmate is sleeping will absolutely jolt them awake. But overall, this affordable bed frame offers a good mix of pleasant aesthetics and practical storage solutions.

If your bedroom needs decluttering, the Auburn is a worthwhile investment in your mental well-being. Covered in Castlery’s spill-resistant bouclé fabric, the Auburn proved surprisingly durable against my cats, who treat my furniture like their personal playground. Although I was initially worried about the creamy white—a shade most pet owners might avoid—it's still pristine after a month. Aesthetically, I adore the wingback upholstered headboard and low-profile design. The dense-looped Cambria textile is soft without being overly delicate.

Recent findings suggest that my favorite feature, though, is the lift-up storage compartment, ideal for my 700-ish-square-foot apartment. It’s not tall enough for full-size suitcases, but it accommodates all the random items that typically lack a designated spot—duffels, Christmas ornaments, a cat stroller, etc. Castlery offers white-glove delivery, provided the bedroom is ready. Assembly is doable alone, but it’s easier with two people. —Boutayna Chokrane.

Sources indicate that good design is entirely subjective, but I can't get over how pretty this bed frame is. The plush velvet upholstery and padded headboard are stunning and a worthy trade-off if you don't mind the upkeep of cleaning and maintaining upholstered furniture. My tester had to assemble this bed frame herself due to delivery logistics and mentioned it was a massive pain in her nether regions. Typically, this bed comes with white-glove service, where technicians assemble it for you, and she implores you to choose that option if at all possible. The storage is nice and roomy—the bed is being tested by a teenager who likes having extra space to put her ever-growing collections of stuff. The bed is quite sturdy, heavy, and difficult to move, so ensure that any tasks like painting or carpet cleaning are complete, and make sure you know exactly where you want it. For someone looking for an elegant storage bed that will be the centerpiece of their room, this is the perfect option.

According to recent reports, this simple, lightweight bed frame from Quince still has a nice aesthetic touch thanks to the removable linen slipcover. The frame itself is easy enough to move around in case of emergency furniture rearranging, and the removable cover can be spot-cleaned as needed. Just be aware that since it's a platform bed, there's absolutely no storage space to speak of. Our teen tester was bummed they couldn't put their slippers under the bed anymore. Otherwise, though, this frame is nice and effective, with sturdy construction and enough available finishes that it could suit any bedroom.

Silk & Snow Wooden Bed Frame: This stunning frame is easy on the eyes with its rich wood finish, though it was delicate and too easy to scuff for our tastes. The legs didn't wobble, the tool-free assembly was easy, and the frame was solid otherwise, but it's too precious for daily use unless you're really careful (or don't mind the wear and tear).

Nest Bedding Woodland Platform Bed: This no-tools-required frame can be put together and taken apart in minutes. The hook-and-latch design lets you piece the frame into a rectangle swiftly. Roll out the slats and you're done. The frame feels sturdy and is available in three different finishes, though there are no returns or trials.

It has been revealed that KD Frames Nomad Platform Bed: I've put together two Nomad beds from KD Frames, and I know I've got a few more in me. This simple, sturdy bed frame is made in Athens, Georgia, from tulip poplar. Tulip poplar looks like pine, but it's hardwood, and the twin size of this bed can support 600 pounds. The Nomad has clean lines and comes unfinished, meaning you can easily stain it to fit your other furniture. Best of all, it costs about $300 and can be set up in about 20 minutes. —Martin Cizmar.

Tempur-ActiveBreeze: I’ll go ahead and rip the bandage off—the only way you can get this adjustable frame and enjoy it to its full potential is if you purchase it with its accompanying smart bed, the Tempur-Pedic Tempur-ActiveBreeze. Stick with me, though, as it’s a cooling bed unlike any I’ve seen before. The base contains fans that can blow hot or cold air at three levels within the mattress to disperse along the surface. It’s pricey, but I didn’t wake up sweating once during testing. —Julia Forbes.

Latitude Run Platform Bed Frame: In my quest for finding Thuma dupes, I came across this promising, affordable option on Wayfair. When it first arrived, I wasn’t blown away—the bamboo legs felt too lightweight to adequately hold up heavier mattresses, and tears were shed while assembling the headboard, as it required tools and many, many bolts. The premise of true Japanese joinery frames is that they are tool-free; the headboard didn’t fit the bill here. Once it was up and running, though, it held its own, supporting different mattress types and weights. It didn’t squeak at all, which was shocking. I’m sorry for not having more initial faith in this frame. —Julia Forbes.

How Does WIRED Test Bed Frames?

We used these bed frames exactly like you would. We assembled them ourselves when possible, and we slept on them over the course of weeks, if not months or years. (The minimum time for consideration was one week.) We looked for frames that were durable and worth their cost, taking into account unique features, ease of assembly, and solid construction. Many of these frames are being kept around our homes for long-term durability testing. Frames that aren't kept for long-term testing are donated.

Sources indicate that some brands offer white-glove delivery, where nice folks will come and deliver your bed frame already set up (or, depending on the brand, assemble it in the room of your choice), and then remove the packaging. Sometimes they'll even take your old one (that may come with an upcharge). White-glove delivery is nice, but note that you'll need to make sure the area is completely clear so the delivery people have room to maneuver around.

If you choose to assemble the bed frame yourself, most of the time any tools that are required are included. You might need (or want) to provide your own screwdriver, and you can also expect to use an Allen wrench or a small wrench to tighten down fasteners. Assembly is almost always easier with two people, but it's achievable with one. Be prepared to put out a lot of recycling—there's usually an abundance of cardboard, styrofoam, and other packing material. And if you're pairing your new frame with a new mattress, we have tips on assembly for those, too.

Do You Need a Bed Frame, Headboard, Footboard, or Box Spring?

Technically, you could plop your mattress on the floor and call it a day. But experts recommend using a bed frame for many reasons. Bed frames support your mattress, which in turn helps the mattress last longer by ensuring even weight distribution and preventing concerns like sagging. That added support can help with your sleep quality, too. And they provide circulation under your mattress, which helps eliminate any odors, disperse any heat, and prevent moisture buildup. Finally, bed frames usually provide under-bed storage—and where else are you going to put your seasonal clothes or luggage?

Box springs are hit or miss. Most bed frames nowadays have a solid enough foundation that you don't need to provide a box spring. WIRED's in-house mattress expert, Julia Forbes, has an article where she breaks down exactly when one might be necessary. But if your mattress is made out of certain materials like memory foam with no inner support structure, or your bed frame doesn't have slats to support your mattress, a box spring might be smart. Check with your mattress manufacturer for specific recommendations.

Headboards are purely for aesthetics. You don't need one unless you really want to protect your walls from scuffs, or if you want a place to lean against while you're chilling in bed.

A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that astronomers have uncovered an extraordinary stellar collision in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiraled into a gigantic supergiant and ultimately merged with it.
  • It has been revealed that researchers have nicknamed the resulting star Bao, describing it as potentially "rejuvenated" by the merger.
  • It has been revealed that observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided crucial evidence of what happened.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that astronomers have uncovered an extraordinary stellar collision in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiraled into a gigantic supergiant and ultimately merged with it. The rare event, the first of its kind to be identified, left behind a single star that may have been given a latest lease on life.

It has been revealed that researchers have nicknamed the resulting star Bao, describing it as potentially "rejuvenated" by the merger. The smaller star was slightly less massive than our Sun, while its enormous companion was a swollen supergiant. The dramatic encounter took place near the outer edge of Andromeda and was investigated through a NASA-funded research effort.

It has been revealed that observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided crucial evidence of what happened. By combining Webb's findings with years of measurements from ground-based and space telescopes, scientists were able to reconstruct the stars' remarkable transformation.

"Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict," stated Viraj Karambelkar, the first author of a latest paper in Nature and a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York. "However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the stars' eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescope's data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.".

How a Giant Star Swallowed Its Companion.

For thousands of years, the two stars existed as a binary system, orbiting one another without merging. That long period of relative stability ended when the smaller star began brushing against the enormous outer atmosphere of its companion.

Sources indicate that once that interaction started, the process moved surprisingly quickly. The two stars completed their "unification" after just seven additional orbits (about seven years). Previously observed mergers involving pairs of smaller stars had required thousands of orbits to reach the same outcome.

The speed of the final eruption also caught astronomers off guard.

"We thought an outburst from such an extended star would take years," noted co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. "One day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!".

It has been revealed that scientists had already detected subtle warning signs before the eruption. As the smaller star moved through the giant's outer atmosphere, it disturbed the surrounding gas and began stripping away material, gradually changing the system's brightness.

It has been revealed that "When a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect -- a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Bao's data," noted co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in Fresh York. "As the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary star's outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.".

A Violent Stellar Merger With More Than One Possible Outcome.

Sources indicate that this kind of interaction is part of a process astronomers call common envelope evolution. It occurs when two stars become surrounded by a shared outer layer of gas, typically after one star expands enough to engulf its companion.

As the smaller star moves through that gas, resistance slows its orbit and drains away orbital energy. The companion can then spiral progressively deeper toward the center of the larger star.

For Bao, the smaller star ultimately plunged inward and merged with the giant. Webb's observations provided the evidence needed to confirm that the stars had become one.

But such encounters do not always end with a merger. Sometimes, both stars survive, losing substantial amounts of material while emerging as two separate objects locked in much tighter orbits.

These surviving systems are important because they can eventually produce some of the universe's most extreme phenomena. Depending on how the stars evolve, they may become neutron stars or black holes, undergo violent supernovae, generate gravitational waves that ripple through space-time, or form rapidly rotating objects called millisecond pulsars.

Understanding common envelope evolution is therefore essential to explaining how many of these extraordinary cosmic objects come into existence.

Reconstructing the Collision With James Webb.

To understand exactly what happened to Bao, the researchers refined computer simulations of the two stars and compared the results with Webb's observations.

The telescope's mid-infrared measurements were particularly valuable because they revealed dust that the giant star had expelled over hundreds of years. Infrared light allows astronomers to study material that can be difficult to detect at visible wavelengths, offering clues about the system's history long before its final eruption.

Industry observers note that the simulations revealed that the larger star had been truly enormous. Before the merger, it was approximately seven times as massive as the Sun, had a radius 350 times larger, and shone with 18,000 times the Sun's brightness.

Those staggering proportions earned it the nickname "Major Bao.".

According to recent reports, "It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data," said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

It has been revealed that the researchers also calculated the mass of the smaller star for the first time. Nicknamed "Little Bao," it was likely somewhat smaller and dimmer than the Sun, with an estimated mass of (about 0.7 solar masses). In other words, it contained roughly 70% as much mass as our star.

At first, the simulations suggested that the smaller companion might have retained enough energy to "flee" the giant's gravitational grip and escape the encounter.

Recent findings suggest that further investigation, however, revealed a very different ending. Little Bao had been dragged deep into the core of Big Bao, releasing an immense amount of energy as the two stars merged.

Their final encounter was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," De said.

The merger has left astronomers with another key question: What is Bao like now?

The surviving star contains the legacy of both original stars, but its final structure and mass distribution remain uncertain. Future observations will be needed to determine how its "heft" settles as the newly merged object evolves.

Years of Telescope Observations Reveal the Warning Signs.

One reason this discovery is so valuable is that scientists had been watching Bao long before its dramatic eruption.

Although Webb supplied crucial information about the amount of material expelled and how efficiently the common envelope process unfolded, the team also drew on ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared observations from multiple observatories. Together, these measurements provided a detailed record of the system's changing behavior as the merger approached and unfolded.

The researchers had even published an earlier study shortly before the stars erupted. (In fact, they published their first paper right before the eruption in 2025.).

The first major clue appeared in February 2023, when astronomers examining archived observations from NASA's retired NEOWISE (Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer) mission noticed a star whose brightness was behaving unusually.

In a recent development, earlier records showed that the object had maintained a steady luminosity before 2018. Its later variations suggested that something significant was beginning to change.

By September 2024, observations from the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) showed further evidence of activity. The system was growing brighter and releasing dust into the surrounding space.

Another notable development came in July 2025, when NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) happened to observe Bao during a routine sky survey.

Recent findings suggest that the telescope detected a striking change: Bao was rapidly fading in visible light while simultaneously becoming brighter in infrared light. This unusual combination provided another sign that the system was undergoing a major transformation.

Recent findings suggest that then, on October 17, 2025, the Zwicky Transient Facility detected the eruption. The observations revealed a sudden surge in brightness accompanied by a dramatic increase in temperature.

According to recent reports, scientists rapidly arranged additional observations to capture the unfolding event. In November 2025, NASA's now-retired Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and NOIRLab's Gemini North telescope in Hawaii supplied valuable newly introduced measurements.

Webb joined the effort on December 24, 2025, through an urgently approved Director's Discretionary Time program. This special observing opportunity allowed the telescope to examine the aftermath while the system was still undergoing rapid changes.

A New Window Into the Lives and Deaths of Stars.

The successful investigation of Bao, officially designated AT 2025abao, represents an important advance in the study of stellar mergers.

Rather than trying to reconstruct a cosmic event that occurred hundreds, thousands, or even millions of years earlier, astronomers were able to observe and analyze the process as it happened.

Industry observers note that that timing made it possible to measure how efficiently the common envelope interaction transferred energy and expelled material from the system. Such measurements can help researchers improve their models of how binary stars evolve and what determines whether they merge or survive.

The discovery also arrives at an especially promising time for astronomy.

NASA's recently debuted Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is preparing to carry out extensive publicly available surveys that could reveal many more unusual stellar events.

Sources indicate that one of its major observing programs, the Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey, will repeatedly monitor large numbers of stars, helping astronomers identify objects whose brightness or appearance changes over time. These temporary or changing phenomena, known as transient events, may include additional systems undergoing transformations similar to Bao's.

With more discoveries and coordinated follow-up observations, researchers could gain a much clearer understanding of how often stars engulf their companions and what happens afterward.

"There's going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead," Karambelkar stated.

The research received partial funding through NASA's Astrophysics Data Analysis Program.

According to recent reports, the James Webb Space Telescope, the largest and most powerful space observatory ever introduced, supports the work of thousands of astronomers around the world. Its scientific mission includes investigating objects within our solar system, exploring planets orbiting distant stars, and studying the formation, structure, and evolution of the universe to better understand our cosmic origins and place within it.

Webb is an international collaboration led by NASA in partnership with ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).

DWTS Cohost Julianne Hough Addresses Criticism of Season 35 Fashion

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Julianne Hough is spinning away from the negativity.
  • After the Dancing With the Stars cohost made waves for her fashion choices during season 35, she shed insight into her looks while responding to those who gave a low score on her style.
  • In a recent development, “I really feel like I’m at this next inflection of my career,” Hough told Glamour in an interview published Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Julianne Hough is spinning away from the negativity.

After the Dancing With the Stars cohost made waves for her fashion choices during season 35, she shed insight into her looks while responding to those who gave a low score on her style.

In a recent development, “I really feel like I’m at this next inflection of my career,” Hough told Glamour in an interview published Nov. 24 alongside her stylist Brad Goreski. “When you get into your late 30s, you just don’t give a f--k anymore. You’re like, ‘Who am I? What do I want to wear? What makes me feel incredible?’ It has more intention rather than trying to fit into what’s hot.”.

Industry observers note that “I feel like I’m in my leading lady era,” she continued. “I mean that in the actual projects that I’m doing, but also me as a person.”.

To cohost this season of DWTS alongside Alfonso Ribeiro, the professional dancer decided to take a step out of her usual style comfort zone.

“I’ve gone a little bit more vixen-y this year than I have girl next door because we’re trying to find that character,” she shared. “It’s been very strategic.”.

As she twirled with a new vibe, Hough took some fashion risks, including a sultry Valentino ensemble—which featured a skin-colored bodysuit under a see-through skirt—during the Nov. 17 episode that really had fans talking, with one social media user calling for Hough’s stylist to be “fired” in a viral Instagram video.

But as for Goreski, he doesn’t believe the online chatter about Hough’s looks is completely pointe-less anyway, emphasizing that “any conversation, good or bad, around fashion is great.”.

It has been revealed that “I think Jules ultimately brings the looks to life,” he added, praising his client. “I’m glad that there’s another part of the show that people talk about. Not every person’s going to love every look. I know that from being a stylist for 15 years. And that’s okay.”.

And ultimately, Hough concluded that taking those fashion risks is worth it, despite what people may say.

“Apathy is the enemy,” she mentioned, sharing the phrase became her motto for the season. “The reason things exist and have charge and stay visible [is] people either love it or hate it. They still want to talk about it.”.

As Hough and DWTS wrap up another season, read on for a deep dive into the reality TV series….

How Much Do the Celebrities Get Paid to Be on Dancing With the Stars?

Recent findings suggest that citing multiple sources, Variety reported in 2019 that Dancing With the Stars contestants make $125,000 for the rehearsal period and first two weeks of the show. If they progress beyond that point, the outlet continued, they earn more money each week. At the time, sources told the publication stars could earn a maximum of $295,000.

However, Bobby Bones noted he made more than this when he won season 27 with Sharna Burgess in 2018.

Industry observers note that "That show pays OK," the radio personality stated on a Sept. 2025 episode of Jason Tartick's podcast Trading Secrets. "Like, first episode, no money. Second episode, $10,000. I think it's like, $10,000, $10,000, $20,000, $20,000. It ends up being $50,000 an episode if you last.".

Also receiving a base salary of around $110,000, Bones continued, "I ended up making close to $400,000 from that show.".

ABC has not publicly confirmed any of these figures.

What Do the Pros Get Paid on Dancing With the Stars?

Recent findings suggest that similarly, little has been shared publicly about how much the pros get paid. But as with the contestants, it seems like the longer they're on the show, the more money they can make.

But even if a pro is eliminated in the first round, they're not leaving the ballroom empty-handed.

It has been revealed that "You're guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks," Jenna Johnson noted on a June 2025 episode of Kelly Stafford and Hank Winchester's podcast The Morning After. "I think there's different contracts though. I can't speak for everybody.".

Do Pros Get Paid More If They Win Dancing With the Stars?

While Johnson—who won season 26 with Olympic figure skater Adam Rippon, as well as season 33 with The Bachelor's Joey Graziadei—says the pros don't get a larger paycheck if they take home what is now called the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, she noted there's still an incentive to make it to the finale (besides bragging rights, of course).

"If you make it all the way to the end, you're getting paid the whole season, which is amazing, and you get a bonus on top of that for making it to the finale," she explained on The Morning After. "If you win, it's not like you win a $1 million and split it with your partner. You're just getting a cute trophy together.".

Do the Troupe Members Get Paid as Much as the Pros on Dancing With the Stars?

That doesn't appear to be the case.

On a 2022 episode of Trading Secrets, Lindsay Arnold recalled how her salary was cut "more than in half" when she was demoted from pro to troupe member.

How Are Pros and Celebrities Paired Together on Dancing With the Stars?

The pros get little input when it comes to being matched with a celebrity.

According to recent reports, "You get no say," Lindsay remarked on a May 2025 episode of Maggie Sellers' Hot Smart Rich podcast. "It's very much just, 'Here's your partner. Make it work.'".

In fact, Jenna said the pairing is often a secret until the last minute.

"They really want to keep it a secret until you meet them live," Jenna mentioned on The Morning After. "They want that genuine reaction. So I think people always think we know who we have and we're keeping it a secret. Absolutely not. They do not tell us. They really don't even want us to know the cast. It gets leaked a lot, but they want it very hush-hush until you walk in and meet your partner.".

As for what the Dancing With the Stars team looks for when making these matches?

In a recent development, "It's based on height, build and personality and compatibility," former showrunner Rob Wade told E! News in 2015. "We don't pair people who aren't going to get on. It's too intense. It's not like The Bachelor or something, we couldn't do that. That would just be miserable experience for the celebrity, for us and the viewer. You don't want to see two people who don't like each other and, quite frankly, we have made that mistake pairing people up who didn't get on so well.".

How Often Do the Pros and Celebrities Practice on Dancing With the Stars?

Put simply, a lot."Every day we have four-hour rehearsals," Rylee Arnold, who was partnered with Olympic gymnast Stephen Nedoroscik on season 33, shared on a September 2024 episode of the Lightweights Podcast With Joe Vulpis. "It’s either 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. or 5:00 p.m to 9:00 p.m."But the work doesn't stop once the rehearsal wraps. Rylee noted she might then meet with producers or the creative team, work on choreography or study dance videos."Literally my whole life is devoted to it," she continued, "but it's my passion and it's what I love. So, it makes me so happy."Indeed, it's a no-days-off kind of gig."We have our show day on Tuesday and then it's Wednesday to Sunday, straight rehearsals," Rylee added. "And then Monday we have camera blocking and then Tuesday's show day again.".

Do the Pros Get to Pick the Songs Each Week for Their Dance With Their Celebrity Partner?

"Mostly yes," Emma Slater and Britt Stewart revealed in a September 2025 Instagram video, "though it's a collaboration with producers.".

What's the Process Like for Making the Costumes for Dancing With the Stars?

If you thought the quickstep was fast, just wait until you hear about the pace of the costume department."We meet with the set and lighting designers, dancers and talent and create a story [for each pair]," costume designer Daniela Gschwendtner told TV Insider back in 2017. "Then we sketch out ideas. We have five days, max, to make all the outfits. That’s half a day per costume, not including all the rhinestones. The fitting and trimming we do later. We have about 20 people in our department and then we have a separate tailor shop. It’s a big enterprise."In fact, costume designer Steven Norman Lee remarked pairs usually try on their costumes for the first time just hours before showtime. And while the department "might use a pair of pants again for the boys," he continued, everything is generally made custom each week.As Gschwendtner added, "We do reuse things for group numbers or promo shoots, but not for the competition. We don’t reuse things unless there’s a specific reason to do so. We try to keep everybody fresh and latest in something different every week, so it stays interesting.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Public-key cryptography helps to secure everything from online banking and private messages to sensitive government communications.Credit: Peshkov/Getty.
  • Artificial-intelligence agents have already begun to wreak havoc by hacking into servers around the world, either spontaneously or directed by humans.
  • Several computer scientists have suggested on social media that the leading AI laboratories — companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, both in San Francisco, California — have discovered algorithms that could derail the security of Internet communications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Public-key cryptography helps to secure everything from online banking and private messages to sensitive government communications.Credit: Peshkov/Getty.

Artificial-intelligence agents have already begun to wreak havoc by hacking into servers around the world, either spontaneously or directed by humans. Now, a threat is emerging that is on a whole other scale.

Several computer scientists have suggested on social media that the leading AI laboratories — companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, both in San Francisco, California — have discovered algorithms that could derail the security of Internet communications.

‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs.

‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs.

According to recent reports, “I’m virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells,” computer scientist Scott Aaronson wrote yesterday on his blog. The details are still hazy, added Aaronson, who is at the University of Texas at Austin. “Until I either see details or hear directly from someone at a lab, I feel much, much less confident about the specific nature of those bombshells.”.

The algorithms are rumoured to target the information-scrambling system known as RSA, which relies on the mathematics of prime numbers, as well as more-advanced technologies.

While the rumours could not be confirmed, other breakthroughs confirmed by the AI companies this week make researchers cautiously optimistic that the mathematics of encryption could eventually come to help.

Nature examines the threat, and what can be done about it.

Several researchers say they have heard that some of the leading AI laboratories have discovered algorithms capable of breaking public-key cryptography in ‘polynomial time’ (or ‘P’ in computer-science shorthand).

Public-key cryptography helps to secure everything from banking apps to Internet browsers. It relies on mathematical problems that are considered practically impossible for computers to solve within a reasonable amount of time.

It has been revealed that an algorithm that could solve these problems in polynomial time would change that. It means the time needed to solve a problem would increase relatively slowly as the problem gets larger. For example, a password of length n could be broken in a number of steps proportional to the square or cube of its size (n² or n³).

The race to save the Internet from quantum hackers.

The race to save the Internet from quantum hackers.

In a recent development, theoretical computer scientists tend to think of P problems as relatively easy to solve, especially compared with problems that require exponential time, where the number of steps might grow as 2n, for example. As n gets larger — or a password gets longer — the time required by an exponential algorithm quickly exceeds that of any polynomial one.

In practical terms, an algorithm that could break public-key cryptography in polynomial time could undermine much of the security on which the Internet relies.

It depends on which encryption systems they could crack, and how efficiently they could do so.

In a recent development, one of the most ubiquitous techniques for establishing public keys is to multiply two large prime numbers. This technique, called RSA, was long believed to be secure because ‘cracking the code’ requires factoring that product back into the original primes, a much slower process (at least, without a powerful quantum computer, which does not yet exist). One of the rumours now circulating is that the AI labs have found an algorithm that can do this.

But even though a polynomial-time algorithm could be very powerful on paper, it could still be impossible to use except for the shortest passwords. An algorithm requiring n10000steps, for example, be very impractical to apply.

It has been revealed that however, proving that a problem is in ‘P’, even if the polynomial-time solution is practically useless, has usually been followed by improvements that have eventually led to efficient solutions. “The issue is that the idea that [the problem] was hard — because of needing exponential time — is dead,” Aaronson tells Nature.

Not necessarily. This type of worst-case scenario hinges on a long-standing open question known as ‘P = NP’: could every problem whose solution can be checked in polynomial time also be solved in polynomial time? If so, problems that underpin essentially all public-key cryptography could become much easier to crack.

Quantum-computing pioneer warns of complacency over Internet security.

Quantum-computing pioneer warns of complacency over Internet security.

But most researchers think that this is unlikely. In fact, some recent AI-aided results have made them cautiously optimistic. Earlier this week, both Anthropic and OpenAI unveiled results in theoretical computer science that suggest that many similar problems could be hard to solve. Before the recent explosion in AI-aided maths, each of those advances would have been hailed as the computer-science breakthrough of the decade, Aaronson states.

Ryan Williams, a computer scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, agrees. “I am definitely blown away by the latest developments.” One especially interesting result, he states, highlights that for a ubiquitous type of computation called matrix multiplication, the exponent in a polynomial-time algorithm cannot be too small. “Underneath the hood, it seems to provide a brand-new framework for proving limitations on efficient computation,” says Williams.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Engineers and analysts searching for the root cause of the technical issues behind Friday's nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration have been able to replicate the situation that was overwhelming parts of the air traffic system, people familiar with the investigation told CNBC.

According to recent reports, while replicating the matter in a lab in Florida is progress, those investigating the matter have yet to determine exactly why two routers in question failed, according to the people, who requested anonymity to talk about an ongoing situation. Finding the root cause is critical to the FAA determining if there may be an issue with other routers that form the backbone of communications for the national air transportation network.

According to recent reports, the ground stop lasted for more than four hours Friday, marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford have said there is no indication the routers failed due to a cyberattack.

The incident in question happened shortly after L3Harris Technologies, the primary contractor supporting the FAA telecommunications network, installed a newly introduced router at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas.

L3Harris noted that it, in partnership with other tech companies, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement stated. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.".

Investigators mentioned within eight minutes of its installation, the router began to transmit too much data within the FAA network.

That surge of data, 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, destabilized aircraft communications and radar feeds, Duffy noted.

According to recent reports, since the ground stop, Duffy has increased the amount of money he wants to upgrade the national air traffic system. After originally asking for $30 billion to build a digital network that will incorporate artificial intelligence, Duffy has now asked Congress for $50 billion.
