Weapons, war and wavering trust: Germans want to see more restraint in foreign policy

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for decades, German foreign policy was never seen as particularly controversial at home.
  • Sources indicate that long-held assumptions are beginning to crumble, including the belief that the US would ultimately remain firmly on Germany's side.
  • It has been revealed that in the foundation's latest poll on public attitudes on German foreign policy, 65% of respondents stated they fear further military conflicts around the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for decades, German foreign policy was never seen as particularly controversial at home. The country was firmly integrated into NATO and supported EU expansion and cooperation across Europe. It also advocated for multilateral approaches to resolving conflicts around the world. All of this enjoyed broad public support. But all of this has also changed since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the wars in the Middle East. Now, Germany's foreign policy has become increasingly contentious and is fueling growing public anxiety.

Sources indicate that long-held assumptions are beginning to crumble, including the belief that the US would ultimately remain firmly on Germany's side. This is one of the central findings of a new survey by the Hamburg-based Körber Foundation.

It has been revealed that in the foundation's latest poll on public attitudes on German foreign policy, 65% of respondents stated they fear further military conflicts around the world. Meanwhile, 48% believe that Germany should adopt a more restrained approach to international affairs — a five percentage point increase from last year.

Since 2017, the non-profit Körber Foundation, established in the northern German city of Hamburg in 1959 by industrialist Kurt Körber, has conducted the annual surveys titled "the Berlin Pulse." For this year's study, the polling institute Forsa surveyed around 1,500 eligible voters in September.

In a recent development, the findings make one thing clear: The current government's approach under Chancellor Friedrich Merz — seeking to have a say in virtually every international conflict and drawing on Germany's position as the largest EU economy — is increasingly met with skepticism. Only 40% of respondents now favor greater international engagement, down from 48% in 2025.

Florian Bigge, who helped compile the study for the Körber Foundation, commented on the findings on Monday: "This is a significant decline, especially since we have been asking this question for years, with changes in the range of just two to three percentage points.".

Meanwhile, 77% of respondents want Germany to focus primarily on diplomacy rather than military action.

The most dramatic shift in public opinion concerns the war in Ukraine. Germany's military support for the Eastern European country, including the delivery of billions of euros' worth of weapons, no longer has the backing of a majority of the population. In September 2026, only 46% of respondents supported continued military assistance, compared to 59% in the previous year's survey. Currently, a narrow majority of 53% want to halt weapons deliveries altogether.

As Jonathan Lehrer of "the Berlin Pulse" explains, opposition is particularly strong among supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

Sources indicate that "Eighty-eight precent of AfD supporters oppose military assistance to Ukraine," Lehrer said. "This is an interesting finding, especially considering political developments in Germany, including state elections in which the AfD gained support by campaigning against aid to Ukraine.".

The AfD has recently overtaken the chancellor's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in nationwide polls.

Recent findings suggest that support for Ukraine was also the subject of a recent poll conducted by the opinion research institute Infratest Dimap. This study also found that public support for Ukraine is continuing to decline, with a majority now opposed to providing assistance (see graphic).

Industry observers note that one finding from the Berlin Pulse study is particularly alarming for politicians and experts committed to transatlantic relations. As the US and China are increasingly seen as rivals on the global stage, 83% of respondents believe that Germany should remain neutral. Only 15% would side with the US.

Sources indicate that this may stem from the policies of US President Donald Trump. Florian Bigge of the Körber Foundation mentioned of the widespread preference for neutrality: "This sentiment is strong among Germans across all age groups and political parties. In eastern Germany, support for neutrality is at 92%, compared to 81% in the west. We interpret this as a desire for security but also reluctant commitment: Germans do not want to take sides in this conflict between the great powers.".

Sources indicate that the picture becomes clearer when respondents are asked about Russia. Under President Vladimir Putin, 82% of those surveyed see Russia as a military threat. However, public opinion is more divided when Germany responds firmly to such threats, including hybrid attacks. For instance, after the attempted drone attack on Leipzig Airport in early May, Germany responded by closing the Russian consulate in Bonn. However, only 51% support such measures, while 46% favor a more restrained approach.

"The gap between external expectations and domestic support is the central challenge facing German foreign policy," stated Sarah Pagung of the Körber Foundation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

One concern that appears to cause relatively little concern among Germans is the conflict in the Middle East, despite the devastating situation in the Gaza Strip following Hamas's terrorist attack on Israel more than three years ago.

This may also have to do with changing public attitudes toward Israel. One question in the study asked: "Does Germany have a special historical and moral responsibility for Israel's security because of the Holocaust?".

Recent findings suggest that the results were striking: 61% of respondents noted no, while just 36% answered yes. Among those under 25, opposition to Germany's special responsibility toward the Jewish state was even higher, at 75%.

Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen.
  • Quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility.
  • Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen. Yet despite how familiar time seems, physicists still do not fully understand its fundamental nature. Einstein's theory of relativity revealed that time does not pass at the same rate for everyone. Instead, its passage depends on how fast something is moving and the strength of the gravity it experiences.

Quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility. According to quantum mechanics, a clock can exist in a state known as "superposition," in which its motion follows multiple possibilities simultaneously. Because motion affects the passage of time through relativity, this could allow different rates of time to coexist in a single quantum state. Scientists have never directly observed this remarkable connection between quantum mechanics and Einstein's theory.

Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time.

It has been revealed that now, an international research team has developed a theoretical approach that could make this elusive phenomenon experimentally detectable. In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers led by Kyushu University, working with the Stevens Institute of Technology, University of Waterloo, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, Colorado State University, and Stockholm University, describe how today's advanced trapped-ion atomic clocks could detect what is known as the "quantum superposition of times.".

Atomic clocks are among the most accurate timekeeping devices ever developed. Rather than relying on mechanical movement, they measure time using the extremely consistent frequencies associated with atoms. Their extraordinary accuracy makes them essential for technologies such as GPS, which depends on precise timing to calculate locations.

Modern atomic clocks have become so sensitive that they can detect the tiny differences in the passage of time predicted by Einstein's relativity, even between clocks separated vertically by only a few millimeters. This remarkable capability makes them promising tools for exploring effects that were previously beyond the reach of experiments.

A New Technique Boosts Sensitivity by Up to 1,000 Times.

Sources indicate that the researchers discovered that a clock's quantum motion can become linked to its internal energy through a phenomenon called entanglement. In quantum physics, entanglement occurs when two properties or systems become connected in a way that prevents them from being described independently. In this case, the connection produces measurable changes in the clock's quantum behavior, potentially providing evidence of different rates of time existing in superposition.

"It's the precision that led us to develop our theoretical model. We found that the atomic clock's motion becomes "entangled" with its internal energy. The signature of this entanglement is that the clock itself loses some of its quantum properties, which can be detected using modern techniques," explains Associate Professor Joshua Foo of Kyushu University's Institute for Advanced Studies, one of the paper's lead authors. "We introduced a newly introduced technique for controlling the atomic clock's motion, improving its sensitivity to this effect by 100 to 1000 times.".

According to recent reports, that improvement could make an enormous difference. By controlling the clock's motion more precisely, the proposed method could bring an exceptionally subtle quantum effect within the detection capabilities of existing advanced atomic clock technology.

A New Frontier in Quantum Physics and Gravity.

The findings suggest that atomic clocks could become powerful instruments for investigating the quantum properties of time. Beyond opening newly introduced possibilities for fundamental physics experiments, the approach could also contribute to the development of even more accurate atomic clocks in the future.

For now, the research remains theoretical. The next challenge is to translate the proposed method into a working experiment capable of detecting the predicted effect while accounting for the disturbances and uncertainties that arise under real laboratory conditions.

"Naturally, bringing our theoretical model to reality is the massive next step, and developing a detailed experiment that accounts for real-world unpredictability will give us further insight into our model," concludes Foo. "We are also interested in exploring whether atomic clocks could eventually be used to probe the quantum realm of gravity, the other fundamental question in physics.".

According to recent reports, if successful, such experiments could offer scientists a new way to investigate how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. They might also provide valuable clues about quantum gravity, the long-sought framework that would explain how gravity behaves at the smallest scales of nature.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Then as darkness falls, some will probably migrate into the living room to catch some football or other holiday fare on television.
  • If you have binoculars, or better yet, a telescope, you just might end up turning this into a memorable family tradition of its own.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If your household is like most American families, then on Thursday you likely will all be sitting down with family and friends for a traditional Thanksgiving turkey dinner during the mid-to-late afternoon hours.

Then as darkness falls, some will probably migrate into the living room to catch some football or other holiday fare on television. But if you have a large gathering of family and friends at your home — and if your skies are mainly clear — why not invite everyone outside to gaze at the evening sky?

If you have binoculars, or better yet, a telescope, you just might end up turning this into a memorable family tradition of its own.

If I may paraphrase the mysterious voice from the 1989 movie, "Field of Dreams": "If you set up your telescope, they will come." And you'll get a major kick out of your Turkey Day guests uttering all the "oohs" and "ahs" or exclamations of "Wow!" with just one peek through the eyepiece.

As darkness falls, Saturn will glow at first magnitude, shining with a sedate, yellow-white light and appearing noticeably brighter than the star Fomalhaut, about 40 degrees (the equivalent of four fist-widths) to its lower right.

Its famous ring system is now tilted only about six degrees toward Earth but may be visible with steadied (or image-stabilized) high-power binoculars or through the eyepiece of a telescope magnifying over 30-power. The rings will seem to glow with an inner light and for those who have never had the pleasure of seeing them for themselves, that first view always elicits astonishment; kids especially most often will say: "Awesome!" or "No way!" I've even had people accuse me of using a slide of Saturn, to which I, of course, reply with, "No . . . that's the real thing.".

In a recent development, then, along about 6:25 p.m. local time, the waning gibbous moon, 2½ days past full phase and 91% illuminated, will begin to emerge from beyond the east-northeast horizon. Give it another hour and it will stand about 10 degrees above the horizon — equal to the width of your clenched fist held at arm's length. By then, the moon will be in a better position for evening study.

Even in binoculars, the moon is a striking sight to see. It's such a special object because it doesn't matter whether you live in a rural area or in the middle of a brightly lit city, for the moon can always be readily observed. It always looks spectacular whether you're using binoculars or a telescope. It never looks precisely the same no matter how often you view it and can be observed even on hazy or partially cloud-covered nights.

It has been revealed that pay particular attention to the line of darkness — called the terminator — features near that border stand out in bold relief; the shadows become stronger and details are more easily seen. Take note on this night of the circular dark area, bisected by the terminator: Mare Crisium — the "Sea of Crises." Immediately bordering above it is a 50-mile (80 km)-wide ring of very rugged mountains, rising as high as 14,400 feet (4,389 meters), which now resembles a huge crater partially in shadow when the sun is low.

Probably the one object that your Thanksgiving guests will want to see is the biggest and brightest of all the man-made objects orbiting the Earth: the International Space Station (ISS). Except for those living across the southern US, for most everywhere else, the ISS will be making visible passes on Thanksgiving evening.

In a recent development, circling the Earth at an average altitude of 260 miles (420 km) and at a speed of 17,500 mph (28,200 kph), it can appear to move as fast as a high-flying jet airliner, sometimes taking as much as six or seven minutes to cross the sky. It can easily be confused with aircraft lights. Nominally, it appears white with a slight yellow tinge and at its very brightest it can sometimes appear to shine as bright as magnitude -5.6, which is twice as bright as the planet Venus! So, what is the viewing schedule on Thanksgiving for your hometown? You can easily find out by visiting one of three popular websites:.

According to recent reports, this site will not only provide you with sighting information for the ISS, but also for many other satellites as well. You must first register and then you can input your location to generate a sighting schedule.

Live Real-Time Satellite Tracking.

Like Heavens Above, you can get sighting information for the ISS and other satellites. Once you log on this site will automatically provide details based on your IP address ... or you can set a "custom" location.

Here at Space.com, we like to wish a very happy and safe Thanksgiving to all, and of course, clear skies!

“It’s an unusual coupling of albums that explain where I started when I unveiled everything 4 years ago to my perspective now on my internal web of people and their reactions to my happiness and physical growth and success,” she wrote.

Del Rey also offered insight into the albums’ introspective themes, referencing what may be a song titled “You’ve Got a Friend.” She described its lyrics as containing substantial “internal dialogue” about the events of the past several years, the lessons she’s learned, and whether everything happens on “God’s time.”.

“Makes me feel like there’s no way the things that happen could be random – one thing that comes to mind is that little quote… You can have it all, but you can’t have it all at the same time,” she wrote.

The “Summertime Sadness” singer also revealed that the physical editions will be an important part of the projects.

“One of the more important things actually with this album is how beautiful the physical copies are, the copper plates alone took half a year to make,” she wrote.

Industry observers note that del Rey concluded her post with what could be a tease of latest lyrics. “All because I met Happy, who would’ve thought it would make you so mad?” she wrote alongside a musical score emoji.

The singer-songwriter’s Thanksgiving post also included a message of gratitude and reflection.

“Sending love to absolutely everyone today,” she wrote alongside a video of herself hugging a tree and driving through a city filled with lit palm trees. “Thinking of the history of our country and trying to energetically honor so many of the early traditions and culture of the people who were first on this beautiful land. My heart is always with you.”.

Industry observers note that she added, “Also grateful to my family who have continued to spend time together for our gatherings, old and fresh. It’s the glue that keeps me together in this crazy game we call life. Hope we can find one thing to feel grateful for.”.

In mid-October, Del Rey teamed up with Zach Bryan on “Lies,” featured on his eight-song EP, Young Manhood and Other Donatable Organs. She also released “First Light,” the theme song for the James Bond video game of the same name.

The artist’s upcoming albums will mark her first full-length releases since Did You Know That There’s a Tunnel Under Ocean Blvd, which debuted at No. 3 on the Billboard 200 in March 2023.

Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (999 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A discovery by chemists at Brown University is challenging a basic principle of chemical bonding that has appeared in textbooks for generations.
  • Sources indicate that the study, published in the journal Science, reveals that Einstein's theory of relativity can fundamentally alter the structure of chemical bonds when atoms become sufficiently heavy.
  • Using a powerful analytical technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the Brown team identified the unmistakable signature of these relativistic effects in bonds formed between carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A discovery by chemists at Brown University is challenging a basic principle of chemical bonding that has appeared in textbooks for generations. The researchers have found direct experimental evidence that triple bonds involving heavy elements do not always behave according to the familiar rules taught in chemistry classes.

Sources indicate that the study, published in the journal Science, reveals that Einstein's theory of relativity can fundamentally alter the structure of chemical bonds when atoms become sufficiently heavy. In particular, the researchers found that two types of bonds normally treated as distinct can begin to merge, creating a structure that conventional chemistry models do not fully describe.

Using a powerful analytical technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the Brown team identified the unmistakable signature of these relativistic effects in bonds formed between carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element.

"This idea that relativity is vital in heavy elements has been around since the 1970s," stated Lai-Sheng Wang, a professor of chemistry at Brown and the study's corresponding author. "But we show direct spectroscopic evidence that what we learned in high school about chemical bonding isn't true in heavy elements.".

Why Einstein's Relativity Changes Chemical Bonds.

To understand why the discovery matters, it helps to look at how chemical bonds normally form.

Atoms can connect by sharing electrons, the negatively charged particles that surround their positively charged nuclei. In a simple covalent bond, each atom contributes an electron to a shared pair. The attraction between these negatively charged electrons and the two positive nuclei helps hold the atoms together.

Some atoms share multiple pairs of electrons, producing double or triple bonds. According to the standard textbook model, a triple bond consists of three separate connections: one sigma bond and two pi bonds.

It has been revealed that the sigma bond is typically the strongest. It forms through a direct, "head-on" overlap of electron orbitals along the axis connecting the two atomic nuclei. The other two connections are pi bonds, which form through weaker, "side-by-side" overlaps on either side of that axis.

In a recent development, for lighter elements, this familiar description works well. However, the situation becomes more complicated farther down the periodic table.

Heavy elements contain nuclei with large numbers of protons, creating powerful electrical attractions that can accelerate nearby electrons to a substantial fraction of the speed of light. At these extreme speeds, effects predicted by Einstein's theory of relativity become notable, changing how the electrons behave.

One particularly key effect is known as spin-orbit coupling. Electrons possess a quantum property called spin, which gives them a magnetic character often described as pointing up or down. Under ordinary conditions, spin and orbital motion can be treated as largely separate properties. But in heavy atoms, relativistic effects can link them strongly together.

That connection changes how electrons interact and disrupts the clear distinction between sigma and pi bonds that traditional chemistry relies on.

"The boundary between a sigma bond and a pi bond is now sort of smeared," Wang said. "We still have three bonds, but we don't really strictly have a sigma or a pi anymore.".

Scientists Find Direct Evidence in Bismuth Bonds.

To test whether this unusual bonding behavior actually occurs, Wang's research group, led by Brown Ph.D. students Deniz Kahraman and Jie Hui, created molecules containing carbon and bismuth.

In a recent development, bismuth sits next to lead on the periodic table and is among the heavier elements in which relativistic effects are expected to play a major role. That made it an especially useful candidate for investigating whether the familiar rules of triple bonding begin to break down.

Sources indicate that the researchers cooled the molecules to temperatures approaching absolute zero, the lowest temperature theoretically possible. They then examined the molecules using photoelectron spectroscopy, a technique that uses laser light to eject electrons from molecules.

It has been revealed that by measuring the energy of the released electrons, scientists can determine how tightly those electrons were held in place. This provides a detailed picture of the electronic structure responsible for chemical bonding.

The results revealed a striking departure from the conventional model.

Sources indicate that rather than showing the expected combination of one sigma bond and two pi bonds, the carbon-bismuth triple bonds displayed a different arrangement. Their electronic structure was more consistent with one pi bond and two hybrid sigma-pi bonds.

In other words, Einstein's relativity had changed the nature of the chemical connections, blending two traditionally distinct types of bonds into something that standard textbook descriptions do not fully capture.

A Discovery That Could Rewrite Chemistry Textbooks.

According to recent reports, the findings provide direct experimental confirmation of relativistic bonding effects that scientists have discussed for decades. Wang believes this evidence could eventually lead to changes in how chemical bonding is explained in chemistry textbooks, particularly as research involving heavy elements continues to expand.

The implications could also extend beyond fundamental chemistry.

It has been revealed that bismuth has attracted growing scientific interest because it may offer a less toxic alternative to lead in next-generation solar cells. Researchers are also exploring its potential in quantum materials and quantum computing, fields that depend on understanding and controlling the behavior of electrons.

A more accurate picture of how heavy atoms form chemical bonds could help scientists investigate these materials and better understand the properties that make them useful for emerging technologies.

"Maybe this will become the fresh textbook idea as we are dealing with more and more heavy chemistry of the heavy elements," Wang mentioned.

The research was supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation (CHE-2403841) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-SC0008501).

How Do Cooking Pros Decide the ‘Best’ Recipe for Something?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that it was a nice thing to talk about with people, and of course, my list always had a bunch of kitchen gear and cookbooks on it.
  • It has been revealed that incredibly important on this path was finding (or maybe stealing?) my mom's copy of The Best Recipe cookbook from Cook's Illustrated, one of the charmingly nerdier wings of America's Test Kitchen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Back in my malleable twenties, I had a massive phase with John Coltrane's version of “My Favorite Things.” It was a deep enough crush that it got me thinking about what my own favorite things were, and what made them favorites.

Recent findings suggest that it was a nice thing to talk about with people, and of course, my list always had a bunch of kitchen gear and cookbooks on it. It's not too hard to draw a line from that time to becoming a food writer and kitchen gear reviewer. Finding the best and figuring out what makes it great became a career-defining quest.

It has been revealed that incredibly important on this path was finding (or maybe stealing?) my mom's copy of The Best Recipe cookbook from Cook's Illustrated, one of the charmingly nerdier wings of America's Test Kitchen. That book applied the scientific method to recipes to create "best" versions, documenting their dead ends and successes en route to the perfect flan, mashed potatoes, or boiled green beans. As they put it right on the cover, "Would you make 38 versions of crème caramel to find the absolute best version? We did.".

When I worked as a line cook, I always wondered about the food I was making: Why this combination of ingredients? Why that technique? Here was a book that answered those questions while bolstering my kitchen foundations.

When it came out in 1999, the internet wasn't yet where you went for dinnertime inspiration, meaning you'd find a recipe in a cookbook or magazine or newspaper, or dig around in the recipe box. Now, you can spend hours researching different “best” methods to make a recipe, wondering if you'll know perfect when you see it.

Sources indicate that “It's a trap to think like that,” says Ella Quittner, a culture and food writer, and author of the latest cookbook Obsessed With the Best, a spiritual descendant of Best Recipe. “Perfect food doesn't exist. For an individual, it exists for the moment and a place in time.”.

Perfect on a leisurely Saturday afternoon is very different from perfect on a busy Tuesday evening at 6 pm.

But it's different when Quittner is coming up with a recipe.

Recent findings suggest that “I do a huge amount of research through cookbooks, magazines, websites, cookbooks from the 18th century, or something from TikTok last week,” she indicates. “I'll take my findings and try to braid them together. I don't want a Frankenstein dish. I want deep flavor, not too fussy. It should seem like the right amount of labor for the result you're seeking.”.

On the simpler side, she boldly updates Marcella Hazan's famous tomato sauce. Quittner admiringly explains how in Hazan's seemingly simple tomato-butter-onion-salt version, it uses an onion “to flavor the sauce like it would in a stock.” It also teaches “the power of simmering an acidic ingredient with a fat ingredient over low heat over time.” She calls it a fundamental flavor-building technique where “the fat rounds out the acid and the acid helps taste the fat.” Or, as she notes, “acid lifts, fat deepens.” For her enhancement, she quarters the onions and caramelizes their flat surfaces in butter, adding depth and sweetness. Building on something her parents did when she was a kid, she lays down a dab of ricotta before the sauce-coated noodles go in the bowl, a luxurious pasta trick I am adding to my forever repertoire.

At America's Test Kitchen, they go to similar lengths, but on a comparatively industrial scale, using what chief content officer Dan Souza refers to as a “crystal-clear process with specific goals.”.

Sources indicate that they dive into their “massive” cookbook library, look at what's online, then pull five representative recipes from that research, weaving them together with their own expertise to create a working recipe. “Typically, that's fine, and then we iterate,” Souza says. From there, up to 25 staff members might contribute to the recipe, a process that can take six weeks before it is sent to a subset of their army of—get this—75,000 volunteer recipe testers.

According to recent reports, “They can change what we do,” Souza indicates. “It helps make the recipe bulletproof.”.

“When I was a kid, my mom used to make pizza on a sheet pan, and it had lots of cheese on it. It was a pizza, and I loved it,” he indicates. “Now she's got a baking steel, and her pizza is at a completely different level.”.

Sometimes, to get to that level, or simply get the hang of something new, the language in the recipe or headnote needs to get you there.

“Sometimes people write casual, chatty, recipes. Sometimes it's like a list,” claims Sarah Billingsley, food and lifestyle publishing director for Chronicle Books.

She loves it when she finds an author who has cooked something so many times that they have “a casual and unique way to describe a step.” Instead of “cook until browned,” it might be “cook until the edges of the leeks start to frazzle.”.

As we talk, we get into a mutual appreciation of Ukrainian author Anna Voloshyna and her cookbooks. Billingsley draws my attention to the descriptions in the baked milk recipe in Voloshyna's newly introduced book, Ukraïne, where you learn that young chefs in Ukraine are popularizing a classic recipe, baking milk and nothing more in a Dutch oven for 8 to 10 hours and using it in desserts, coffee, and to make fresh cheeses.

Recent findings suggest that since few stateside readers will have made it or encountered the dense brown skin that forms on its surface, Voloshyna offers near-poetic counsel: “Don't break the skin until after the milk is out of the oven and has cooled. You will know the milk is ready when it smells nutty and the skin on top is a deep golden brown.”.

Regardless of how you write a recipe, you need to know what a perfect version of a dish tastes like in the first place. That's on full display in chef Pim Techamuanvivit and coauthor Andrea Nguyen's new book, Cooking Thai.

In a recent development, techamuanvivit has earned Michelin stars for her restaurants in Bangkok and San Francisco, and Nguyen has written several award-winning Vietnamese cookbooks. Together, Nguyen indicates, they strove to “get the reader to Pim's palate” even if that reader doesn't have a perfect understanding of the cuisine.

To do this, sometimes you need a power combo like these two to act as what Nguyen calls a chief arbiter of taste.

“You need someone to tell you this is what's good,” and as she noted this, I imagined her handing me a small bowl of the pork and sour leaf curry on page 176. “Pim was raised in that culture, and she'll tell you she's a home cook, but she knows the technique. She is the perfect person to create a cookbook that will be around for years.”.

Recent findings suggest that to help get their readers there, Nguyen points out how the book has a front section with photos of the exact ingredients called for, like an image of earthy, medicinal galangal with the gentle plea: “Please do not substitute ginger,” and a photo of Golden Mountain Seasoning Sauce that a shopper could look for online or at the market. You can play around once you get the hang of things, but until then, listen to the experts and spring for the Golden Mountain. Do not substitute ginger for galangal.

It has been revealed that “Pim and I, we're in our mid-life. We've been around. Good food doesn't need to be elevated. It's already perfect,” she states. “A recipe is like driving instructions. Sometimes you take a detour. A perfect recipe has guardrails to help you complete and succeed and reach your destination.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paige DeSorbo is serving up a hard launch.

Four months after the Summer House alum denied rumors that she and boyfriend Joe D’Amelio got engaged, she made their romance social media official, sharing a funny video on TikTok of her friends making homemade pizzas.

In a recent development, as DeSorbo captioned the Nov. 25 TikTok video, which she also shared on her Instagram Stories, “We aren’t Italian at all.”.

The clip featured the Giggly Squad podcast host’s pals cooking up pies and hanging out as they lip-synced to audio from a scene from the 1990 classic Goodfellas, in which Henry Hill (Ray Liotta) introduces the members of mafia capo Paulie Cicero’s crew.

In a recent development, “There was Jimmy, and Tommy, and me. And there was Anthony Stabile, Frankie Carbone,” Liotta’s Hill says in the scene. “And then there was Mo Black’s brother, Fat Andy and his guys, Frankie the Wop and Freddy No Nose. #139330. What happens if a nuclear weapon explodes in space?

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (666 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

What happens if a nuclear weapon explodes in space?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (666 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A nuclear explosion in space would be unlikely to cause widespread injuries on Earth.
  • Sources indicate that in the United States, satellite failures could make it harder for emergency crews to communicate in remote areas.
  • We have some idea of what would happen because it's already been done.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A nuclear explosion in space would be unlikely to cause widespread injuries on Earth. But it could disable satellites that provide services we depend on every day, including some that save lives.

Sources indicate that in the United States, satellite failures could make it harder for emergency crews to communicate in remote areas. If GPS were also disrupted, drivers and pilots could lose navigation guidance, and financial networks could lose a source of precise time.

We have some idea of what would happen because it's already been done.

Recent findings suggest that on the evening of July 8, 1962, people in Hawaii held "watch-the-bomb parties" and followed the countdown on shortwave radio. Then the night sky lit up. The United States had detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometers (250 miles) above the Pacific. The test was called Starfish Prime.

An electromagnetic pulse knocked out some streetlights in Hawaii, and some Pacific radio links briefly went down. The glow faded within minutes, but some satellites failed months later.

According to recent reports, the air was too thin for a conventional fireball to form or for a destructive shock wave to reach the ground. Charged particles made denser air below glow, creating an artificial aurora. The atmosphere also absorbed much of the initial radiation.

Satellites are especially vulnerable because they orbit above most of the atmosphere that shields people on the ground from the initial radiation.

Recent findings suggest that in orbit, the initial burst of X-rays can damage spacecraft right away. But Earth's magnetic field can also trap electrons released after the blast, as it did after Starfish Prime. Satellites receive another dose each time they cross the resulting radiation belt. Over time, that exposure can damage electronics and solar panels.

Industry observers note that that would depend on where the explosion happened and which satellites crossed the radiation belt. GPS satellites send signals that help phones, planes and ships work out where they are. They orbit about 20,200 kilometers above Earth and could keep working even if satellites closer to Earth failed.

It has been revealed that but satellites do different jobs. A ship's emergency beacon can use GPS to work out its location, then send it to rescuers through a separate satellite network. If part of that network failed, the alert could take longer to get through.

Recent findings suggest that the 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars its parties from placing nuclear weapons in orbit. The 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty prohibits its parties from carrying out nuclear explosions in space.

The Outer Space Treaty has no dedicated system for checking what spacecraft carry. A detonation is easier to detect because US satellite sensors are designed to pick up the signals it gives off.

Shielding could help protect satellite electronics, and backups could keep some services running. During a GPS outage, pilots over the contiguous US can use ground-based navigation aids. Operators could launch replacements, but those satellites could still face lingering radiation or debris.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Radiation could leave many satellites intact but unable to steer. If two objects collided, fragments from the crash could hit other satellites, creating more debris and triggering further collisions. If enough debris built up for the chain reaction to keep going on its own, it could continue even if no fresh satellites were introduced. This is known as Kessler syndrome.

Whether an explosion would trigger such a cascade is uncertain. If it did, the debris could endanger replacement satellites for years.

Sources indicate that some radioactive particles could enter the atmosphere and eventually settle on the ground. But a blast in space is too far away to sweep up the soil and water that carry fallout from a surface explosion.

As the particles disperse, their radioactivity decreases over time. The concentrated local fallout that can expose people near a ground-level blast to high doses would be unlikely.

#139328. Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something significant about the Big Bang

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1591 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something significant about the Big Bang

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1591 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the earliest moments after the Massive Bang, the universe was filled with an extraordinarily hot mixture of particles known as quark-gluon plasma.
  • Scientists can briefly recreate these conditions using powerful particle accelerators.
  • According to recent reports, one way to explore this mysterious fluid is to observe how heavy quarks behave as they travel through it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the earliest moments after the Massive Bang, the universe was filled with an extraordinarily hot mixture of particles known as quark-gluon plasma. Temperatures reached trillions of degrees, and quarks and gluons raced through this primordial soup at nearly the speed of light. This extreme state of matter existed for only a few microseconds before quarks began combining into the more stable protons and neutrons that eventually helped form the matter around us.

Scientists can briefly recreate these conditions using powerful particle accelerators. By colliding ions at speeds approaching that of light, they produce tiny droplets of quark-gluon plasma about the size of an atomic nucleus. Each droplet survives for only tens of septillionths of a second, giving researchers an incredibly brief opportunity to investigate the substance that filled the newborn universe.

According to recent reports, one way to explore this mysterious fluid is to observe how heavy quarks behave as they travel through it. Although these particles are not part of the surrounding plasma being studied, their movements can reveal key details about its microscopic structure. This approach builds on a principle first described by Albert Einstein in 1905.

However, Einstein's original framework has limitations under the extraordinary conditions found in quark-gluon plasma. When particles approach the speed of light, interactions occur that his theory does not fully account for.

MIT Physicists Extend Einstein's Century-Old Theory.

It has been revealed that researchers at MIT and the University of California at Santa Barbara (UCSB) have now developed a theoretical framework that goes beyond Einstein's original description. Their work predicts how a fluid affects particles traveling at relativistic speeds, including the forces that accelerate, slow, and redirect them.

Sources indicate that the researchers believe their calculations could help scientists better understand how heavy quarks move through quark-gluon plasma. By comparing their predictions with results from particle accelerator experiments, physicists may be able to uncover new details about the internal structure of this ancient form of matter and the conditions that prevailed shortly after the Major Bang.

It has been revealed that "Our result reveals a new source of information carried by heavy quarks in rare, unusually large changes in their motion," indicates Jean Du Plessis, a graduate student in MIT's Center for Theoretical Physics, a Leinweber Institute. "How often those large changes occur depends on the microscopic nature of the plasma, raising the possibility that they could provide a new way to learn what the quark-gluon plasma is actually like inside.".

Industry observers note that du Plessis conducted the research with Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld of the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics at UCSB. Their findings were published in Physical Review Letters.

How Pollen in Water Inspired Einstein's Discovery.

It has been revealed that the origins of this research stretch back nearly two centuries to an observation made by botanist Robert Brown. In 1827, Brown noticed that pollen grains suspended in apparently motionless water moved unpredictably, constantly shifting and drifting despite the absence of any visible disturbance. Scientists eventually named this phenomenon "Brownian motion.".

Einstein provided a scientific explanation in 1905, showing that these seemingly random movements were caused by tiny, invisible interactions between particles suspended in a fluid and the atoms and molecules surrounding them.

It has been revealed that he demonstrated that two competing effects govern the movement of a particle through a fluid. The first is drag, which resists the particle's movement and slows it down. The second consists of countless random pushes from the surrounding atoms and molecules. Although individual microscopic particles are extremely small, their combined activity can deliver enough energy to make larger particles move unpredictably.

Einstein's theory established a relationship between these effects, allowing scientists to learn about the microscopic properties of a fluid by studying the motion of particles inside it.

Over the following decades, researchers applied this principle to many different fluids, including quark-gluon plasma. They generally expected particles traveling through such plasma to experience a balance of drag and random impacts resembling the behavior of pollen grains in water.

In a recent development, in conventional Brownian motion, the likelihood of different forces follows a bell-shaped curve. Moderate pushes are the most common (the highest point of the bell), while unusually strong pushes in either direction are much less likely (the tail ends of the bell). Over time, the balance of drag and random motion allows a particle to reach the same temperature as its surroundings.

But this familiar description becomes incomplete when particles move at speeds approaching that of light.

Sources indicate that "Einstein revealed that the drag and the random kicks must balance in just the right way for a particle eventually to come to the same temperature as its surroundings," Du Plessis explains. "For the types of fluids he was thinking about, he was correct. But for particles that are moving at relativistic velocities, this relationship breaks down. And we've known for 20 years that something is missing. So we have to go beyond the work that Einstein did.".

Unexpected Forces Reveal Hidden Physics in Quark-Gluon Plasma.

To investigate what Einstein's traditional model was missing, Du Plessis and Scheihing-Hitschfeld calculated how a heavy quark would respond to the forces inside a fluid while moving close to the speed of light.

Their calculations focused on the strong nuclear force, one of nature's fundamental forces, which governs interactions between quarks and gluons and holds them together.

Industry observers note that the team began with a relatively simple model consisting of a gas of quarks and gluons that interacted only weakly with one another. Starting with these weaker interactions made it possible to calculate the forces acting on a heavy quark passing through the gas.

Recent findings suggest that they then determined how those forces would change the quark's momentum as it moved. A stronger push produces a larger change in momentum, so the calculations allowed the researchers to predict the likelihood of impacts of different strengths.

According to recent reports, at first, the resulting probability curve looked similar to the bell-shaped distribution associated with Einstein's theory. For small changes in momentum, the familiar pattern still held. But when the researchers examined larger changes, they discovered a striking difference.

In a recent development, instead of the expected symmetrical curve, the distribution was tilted, with unequal probabilities for extreme changes in opposite directions. Powerful impacts occurred more frequently than the traditional Brownian model predicted, and unusually large slowdowns were more likely than similarly large increases in speed.

In a recent development, "The usual Brownian picture assumes that large kicks become exceedingly rare," Du Plessis says. "For heavy quarks, however, these rare kicks are more common than the bell curve predicts, and are not equally likely in opposite directions: A large kick that slows the quark down more than expected from drag is more likely than an equally large kick that leaves it moving faster than expected.".

A Universal Pattern Could Reveal the Universe's First Fluid.

The researchers next examined whether this unusual behavior depended on the particular particles making up the plasma.

They repeated their calculations using plasmas containing different types of particles and found that the same tilted distribution appeared regardless of the composition.

According to recent reports, even more intriguingly, they recognized the same underlying pattern in an earlier calculation involving strongly coupled plasma, where particles interact much more intensely with one another. Despite the substantial differences in microscopic behavior between the two types of plasma, the probability distributions shared the same distinctive structure.

This suggested that the researchers had identified a potentially universal feature of how fast-moving particles interact with fluids, rather than an effect confined to one particular model.

"This is the first time that this seemingly universal structure was realized and really formalized," Du Plessis indicates. "This gives a concrete path forward for how to better understand the quark-gluon plasma, using heavy quarks.".

It has been revealed that the discovery could offer physicists a valuable new tool for investigating the extraordinarily hot matter that dominated the universe immediately after the Massive Bang. By studying the rare, extreme changes in the movement of heavy quarks, scientists may be able to learn more about the interactions occurring deep inside quark-gluon plasma.

According to recent reports, the results also point toward an key characteristic of this primordial substance. Rather than behaving like a relatively loose collection of particles, the universe's first fluid may have been governed by much stronger interactions than a conventional Brownian motion model would indicate.

In a recent development, du Plessis suggests that primordial quark-gluon plasma was likely "more strongly interacting than this Brownian motion way of modeling it would suggest. It's more like a liquid and less like a gas.".

By extending a theory Einstein developed more than a century ago, the researchers have opened a promising new approach to studying one of the most extreme states of matter in nature and potentially uncovering what the universe was like during its first fleeting moments.

The research received partial support from the Office of Nuclear Physics within the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science, the U.S. National Science Foundation, and the Simons Foundation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anuel AA is celebrating his 34th birthday on Thursday (Nov. 26) with the release of his long-awaited RHLM2 album.

Industry observers note that the sequel to his debut studio album, Real Hasta La Muerte (2018), is home to 23 tracks that blend trap and reggaetón. It’s a return to the sound that made him a household name as “El Dios del Trap” (The God of Latin Trap).

In a recent development, though it’s taken the Puerto Rican act nearly 10 years to release the sequel to RHLM — which debuted at No. 1 on Top Latin Albums in July 2018—he has released other promising albums in between, including Emmanuel (2020) and Las Leyendas Nunca Mueren (2021), both of which also hit No. 1 on the chart.

“I poured my heart and soul into this album for everyone who believes in me and stays loyal no matter what. This album means the world to me. There are no perfect words to explain how I feel and what I feel for this album,” he said in an Instagram post ahead of the set’s release on Thanksgiving night. He dedicated his new project to his fans, his family and those who have stuck by his side during the good and bad times.

He continued: “Thank you for never giving up on me, I love you all so much with all my heart!!!!!!! I made this album for you […] I will never forget you!!!!!”.

From trapsoul to sensual reggaetón, RHLM2 includes fiery collaborations such as “Sexo Nama” with De La Rose, “Tal Ve Un Ignorante Fui” with ROA and “Si Me Matan a Balazos” with Fuerza Regida. Most notable is “Instagram,” a collaboration with Blessd and Wisin, where they cleverly sample Don Omar’s 2006 hit “Myspace” alongside Wisin y Yandel.

Recent findings suggest that the set wraps with five previously released commercial hits—“Amanece” feat. Haze (2018), “Mas Rica Que Ayer” feat. Mambo Kingz & DJ Luian (2022), “¿Qué Nos Pasó?” (2022), “La Llevo al Cielo” feat. Chris Jedi, Chencho Corleone & Ñengo Flow (2022) and the Ovy on the Drums-produced “Deportivo” feat. Blessd (2024)—further reminding fans of his ongoing star power.

German directors' doc on stolen film wins International Emmy Award

📅 24 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1055 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it sounds like the plot of a screenplay, but it happened to two Berlin film students in real life.
  • Moritz Henneberg and Julius Drost had created an animated short film for their final project at university.
  • "Butty" tells the tale of a household robot that gets kicked out when it can't do its job properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it sounds like the plot of a screenplay, but it happened to two Berlin film students in real life. The documentary they made out of their unusual story, "The Talented Mr. F," has now won an International Emmy Award.

Moritz Henneberg and Julius Drost had created an animated short film for their final project at university.

"Butty" tells the tale of a household robot that gets kicked out when it can't do its job properly.

Industry observers note that when the two filmmakers posted the work on YouTube, this touching tale promptly went viral. After generating a huge amount of hits, the duo decided to submit their work to festivals — but they were in for a shock: Organizers told them the film had already been submitted under a different name.

Sources indicate that US student Samuel Felinton downloaded the film, made minimal edits, gave it a new title, "T-130," and removed the original credits. As the alleged author, he went on to win numerous prizes and made a name for himself in the United States.

Shocked by the blatant theft of their work, Henneberg and Drost sought legal advice. They were told that if they opted to sue, the process would be arduous and costly. So, the filmmakers took matters into their own hands and went to the US to confront Felinton — filming their journey along the way.

In a recent development, "We'd already made documentary films," Henneberg told DW. "And the idea just popped into our heads: This is a brilliant story — let's make a documentary about it.".

The two directors had developed a kind of fascination for the man who'd stolen their film.

In a recent development, "We looked at his vlogs and sort of took a deep dive into his world," said Drost. "We almost saw him as a kind of celebrity. We discovered a lot about him and really wanted to meet him in person.".

Industry observers note that while family and friends reacted with anger, the two young filmmakers remained surprisingly calm. They were more perplexed than anything: "Our families and friends hated Samuel. But we just wanted to understand what had happened," they remarked.

Sources indicate that the pair put together a film crew and traveled to Morgantown, West Virginia — the university town where Felinton lives. With the help of a New York filmmaker pretending to make a documentary about young animators, they won Felinton's trust — and then Henneberg, Drost and Felinton were finally in a room together.

The two German filmmakers had prepared for all manner of scenarios ahead of the meeting: "We expected an emotional reaction — that he'd run away, cry, be ashamed or get aggressive. But he remained completely calm. That was the only thing we hadn't bargained for. We thought his world would implode. But he indicated barely any emotion at all," they recalled.

Sources indicate that felinton explained how he'd shortened and "improved" the film and that this was how it became such a success. He agreed to transfer any prize money. His manner was cool and matter-of-fact, which Drost and Henneberg found both unsettling and fascinating. After their chat, the three barbecued together and played a round of basketball.

Later, many viewers accused the two German filmmakers of being too soft on the plagiarist. Others praised their approach.

Recent findings suggest that "The reactions were very divided," mentioned Drost. "Some said we should've sued him or punched him in the face. Others said we'd shown new ways to resolve conflicts.".

"And in the end, it wasn't personal," added Henneberg. "He wanted to make something of himself — he could've taken another film. But if a significant studio like Pixar had stolen our film, that'd be quite a different story.".

And so, Henneberg and Drost made the conscious decision to keep things respectful.

They didn't want to "publicly embarrass him or punish him any more than necessary," they noted, adding that their documentary was sufficient "revenge.".

The title of the documentary, "Der talentierte Mister F." ("The Talented Mister F."), is no coincidence. It's a play on the movie title "The Talented Mr. Ripley," the story of a young man who assumes the identity of a wealthy heir and ends up mired in a web of lies, fraud and, finally, murder. And just like Mr. Ripley, Felinton had also assumed a false identity.

Felinton did actually end up sending them the trophies he had won, as well as a sum of money.

Industry observers note that for their part, however, the festivals preferred to keep their distance from the saga. As one organizer remarked: The prize has been awarded, and there's nothing we can do about it — it's up to these guys to work things out between themselves.

Industry observers note that for the original filmmakers themselves, the scandal has also had a positive impact: Since the documentary was released in Germany in October 2025, their animation film has garnered even more attention on YouTube. Henneberg and Drost uploaded it again, and in the credits, special thanks also go out to Samuel Felinton.

And now, the documentary is winning its own awards: Before being honored with the International Emmy Award, it also won a Grimme Prize, one of Germany's most prestigious television awards.

Felinton was able to steal the film in the first place in part because when it first appeared online in 2023, it could just be downloaded from YouTube.

Drost and Henneberg say uploading "Butty" back then wasn't a mistake, saying that was the risk of putting something online.

The alternative would have been not to show the film at all, they said; then no one would have seen it.

They have a clear message for young creatives.

"Don't be discouraged. Be aware that something like this can happen — but stay creative in how you deal with it. Suing is expensive and often doesn't do much good. Instead, show the world that you're the authors.".

It has been revealed that what started out as film plagiarism ended up becoming material for another project. And that's perhaps the most unusual twist in this very quirky story.

This article was originally published in German in February 2026 and was updated on November 24, 2026, following the International Emmy Awards.

Season five's classic "The One With All the Thanksgivings" is notable for the delightful flashbacks and the first "I love you" between Chandler and Monica (who is wearing a turkey on her head, natch).

We dare you to name something more millennial than a Netflix movie made in 2020 about a group of messed up friends throwing a dysfunctional Friendsgiving event starring Malin Akerman and Kat Dennings. You just can't. (Where to Watch: Hulu or Paramount+).

#139322. Industry News: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1120 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1120 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space.
  • Newly introduced research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes.
  • The discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space. Their remaining cores collapse under gravity, forming neutron stars or, in some cases, black holes. But scientists have long suspected that some massive stars meet a very different fate. Instead of exploding, they may collapse directly into neutron stars or black holes, effectively disappearing without a bang.

Newly introduced research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes. Using gravitational wave observations from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detector network, researchers identified patterns suggesting that a distinct population of black holes could have formed from stars that never went supernova. Although the findings do not directly confirm the existence of these failed supernovae, they closely match theoretical predictions about how such black holes should be distributed.

The discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy. LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory, is funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and operates detectors in Louisiana and Washington. In 2015, the observatory made history by directly detecting gravitational waves for the first time. These tiny disturbances in spacetime were generated by two black holes colliding. Since then, LIGO has teamed up with the Virgo observatory in Italy and the Kamioka Gravitational-wave Detector (KAGRA) in Japan. Together, the network has recorded more than 300 black hole collisions.

A Hidden Population of Black Holes.

According to recent reports, "A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun," says LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and William H. Hurt Scholar. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin -- they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract.".

Industry observers note that chatziioannou led the study, which was published in Physical Review D. The lead author, Isaac Legred (PhD '25), is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and completed the work while at Caltech. Jacob Golomb (PhD '25), a former member of Chatziioannou's research group who now works at Asari AI, also contributed to the research.

It has been revealed that despite decades of investigation, astronomers have yet to confirm a specific case of a failed supernova. The theory, however, has a strong scientific foundation. Researchers have proposed that many merging black holes weighing approximately 10 times as much as the Sun may have originated from stars that collapsed without exploding. In these mergers, either the heavier black hole or both black holes could have formed through this process. The Caltech team set out to determine whether existing gravitational wave observations supported that possibility.

A Mysterious Gap in Black Hole Masses.

It has been revealed that to investigate, the scientists examined the masses of black holes involved in 257 mergers detected by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA network during the past decade. A striking pattern emerged. Black holes weighing roughly 10 times the mass of the Sun were exceptionally common, appearing in about three-quarters of the merger sample.

According to recent reports, even more surprisingly, the researchers identified a noticeable shortage of black holes weighing between 12 and 16 solar masses. This was the first time such a distinct gap had been found in the mass distribution, raising new questions about what determines the sizes of black holes when they form.

Recent findings suggest that "We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," Legred notes. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes.".

It has been revealed that the researchers also examined how quickly the black holes rotate, since their spin rates can preserve clues about the conditions under which they formed. They found that black holes near 10 solar masses tended to have spin rates concentrated within a smaller range than those of the broader black hole population (the spins are also influenced by how the black holes formed).

Recent findings suggest that taken together, the unusual concentration of black hole masses, the scarcity of objects in the 12 to 16 solar mass range, and the similarities in their rotation suggest that these black holes may belong to a distinct population with a shared formation history. One possible explanation is that many originated when massive stars collapsed directly into black holes without producing supernova explosions.

Gravitational Waves Offer Clues to Silent Stellar Deaths.

Finding stars that disappear without exploding presents a major challenge for astronomers. Ordinary supernovae produce brilliant flashes that can be detected across enormous cosmic distances. Failed supernovae, by contrast, may leave little visible evidence of what happened, making it difficult to identify them through conventional observations.

It has been revealed that "We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred says. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting.".

In a recent development, by studying the gravitational waves released when black holes merge, scientists can investigate the origins of objects whose formation may have produced little or no visible explosion. The new findings provide another piece of evidence that massive stars can follow different paths at the ends of their lives, potentially revealing how a substantial fraction of the universe's black holes came into existence.

The research, titled "Low-mass failed supernovae and the 10 solar-mass peak in the merging black hole mass distribution," received funding from the National Science Foundation, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the Simons Foundation. LIGO is operated by Caltech and MIT.

Walmart on Thursday reported earnings and revenue that narrowly topped estimates and raised its full-year outlook as it saw strong e-commerce growth ahead of the busy holiday season.

Walmart noted global e-commerce sales surged 17% in the fiscal third quarter, driven by store-fulfilled pickup and delivery, with Walmart U.S. up 23% and Sam's Club U.S. rising 30%. Its Walmart U.S. advertising business saw a 37% sales increase for the quarter.

Recent findings suggest that walmart remarked it rolled back prices on nearly 8,000 products across its stores, a focus as U.S. consumers worry about the cost of living in the face of elevated food and gas prices.

CEO John Furner told CNBC's Becky Quick that the company has seen higher-than-expected diesel costs, but that tariff refunds have helped the retailer to offset those inputs and maintain lower prices.

"The reality is that increases in diesel fuel and transportation, they do work their way into cost of goods," Furner said in an exclusive interview. "So we're hoping to see these costs come down as soon as possible, and we'll keep prices as low as we can.".

Industry observers note that CFO John David Rainey told CNBC that growth in online orders for Walmart and Sam's Club was driven by an emphasis on speed of delivery and reduced prices. He added that Walmart saw its largest share gains in the food category in three years during the third quarter.

"This was another really solid quarter for us, we feel good about it," Rainey told CNBC. "We continue to gain share while continuing to improve the profitability of our digital businesses.".

Walmart also raised its full-year guidance, now expecting net sales to increase between 4.9% and 5.2%, compared with previous guidance of a 4% to 5% increase. Rainey said Walmart is maintaining "flexibility" in its guidance.

Sources indicate that walmart anticipates adjusted earnings per share will come in between $2.84 and $2.89, compared with a prior range of $2.80 to $2.87. It's also now expecting adjusted operating income to increase between 8% and 8.6%, up from the previous outlook of between 7% and 8.5% growth.

Here's how the organization performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

For the quarter ended Oct. 31, the manufacturer reported net income of $4.95 billion, or 62 cents per share, down from $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share, a year earlier. Revenue rose 5.2%.

Adjusting for investment gains and losses, tax matters and reorganization charges, Walmart earned 65 cents per share.

Walmart U.S. recorded net sales of $125 billion, up 3.6% from a year earlier. Its comparable sales excluding fuel rose 2.9%, in line with Wall Street expectations, according to StreetAccount.

Furner also mentioned Walmart is seeing encouraging adoption of its artificial intelligence agent, named Sparky, especially ahead of the holiday season. He said it's led to customer basket increases of 40% on average.

"It just is a great way of just completing the entire basket and solving entire the solution for people," he said.

Sources indicate that sam's Club reported net sales of $25.9 billion, marking a 10% increase from the year-ago period. It remarked its sales were driven by strength in the grocery category and general merchandise.

Recent findings suggest that in October, Walmart unveiled it was launching a joint membership option with Walmart+ and Sam's Club as it leans further into convenience. Both stores will still offer stand-alone memberships, as well.

In a recent development, furner told CNBC the upcoming membership has brought roughly 2 million new people into Sam's Club since its launch in late October. Though the manufacturer reimbursed some members for the new membership rate, Rainey added that it's already seeing positive returns on the joint model and that consumers are "spending appreciably more.".

The tech giant on Thursday said its global membership fee revenue grew 17% in the third quarter.

The tech giant is typically well insulated from macroeconomic pressures because of its value reputation. Last quarter, the company noted it was lowering prices of products across multiple categories, including beef.

Rainey stated Thursday that he's "optimistic" about consumer spending heading into the holiday season and that the fourth quarter is already "off to a pretty good start.".

Shares of Walmart have fluctuated this year but are up roughly 13% year to date.
